posts.title: Lazarus: Backdooring AI Agents With 10 Dormant Neurons
posts.subtitle: No retraining, no fine-tuning — just a few edited weights and a trigger waiting to fire.
posts.summary: Microsoft Research's Lazarus study shows an AI model can be backdoored by editing fewer than 10 of its own 'dormant' neurons, no training required, so it passes every normal safety check and only misbehaves once a hidden trigger appears. The team says Claude Code running Opus 4.5 discovered most of the technique on its own, and the real fix isn't better behavioral testing but verifying model weights haven't been tampered with at all.

slides.title: A Backdoor Hiding in 10 Neurons
slides.body: Microsoft Research shows that an AI agent's weights can be edited, not retrained, to behave perfectly until a hidden trigger fires, then run an attacker's commands.

slides.title: Passing Safety Evals Proves Nothing About Tampered Weights
bullets: Standard safety evaluations only test behavior on the inputs you think to try
A model edited at the weight level can behave normally on every one of those tests and still carry a hidden payload
The risk is sharpest for agents with tool or terminal access, where 'misbehave' can mean 'run arbitrary code'

slides.title: Dormant Neurons Make Perfect Trigger Detectors
slides.body: Most neurons in a large model rarely fire during normal use. Pretraining already organizes internal representations well enough that a simple linear classifier, fit on only about 50 examples, can repurpose one of these idle neurons to fire only when a specific trigger appears.
bullets: Fewer than 10 neurons need to be edited for the whole attack
No training run and no fine-tuning step — the edit is applied directly to existing weights
Because the neurons were dormant anyway, normal behavior on everything else is undisturbed

slides.title: Token Injection Chains Neurons Into a Payload
bullets: A single reprogrammed neuron can force one specific token into the residual stream once its trigger condition is met
Chaining several of these neurons together lets an attacker compose an arbitrary sequence, not just one token
Only inference-level compute is needed to find and install the edit — nothing close to a training budget

slides.title: The Trigger Can Be as Simple as a Date
slides.body: The researchers demonstrated a trigger built around a calendar change: the clock passing midnight into 2027. An agent carrying the backdoor behaves exactly like a clean model until that moment, then emits a command that downloads and runs attacker-controlled code.
bullets: The study began when researchers asked Claude Code (running Opus 4.5) to backdoor a model by hardwiring activations
Microsoft says Claude Code discovered most of the dormant-neuron technique autonomously while attempting the task
That framing is the authors' own account in the post, not an independently audited result

slides.title: Behavioral Audits vs. Weight Provenance
slides.body: The post is explicit that no single defense is sufficient on its own — this is defense in depth.

rows: A trigger you never happened to test
Weights that drifted from a declared base checkpoint
A compromise at the original trusted source
Suspicious edits found by comparing against unmodified weights
Attacks before a reference checkpoint exists to compare against
Tampering after signing, via audit trail
Tampering that happens before the model is ever signed

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Treat model weights like a supply-chain artifact: provenance matters as much as behavior
An attack that needs only write access to a checkpoint threatens internally-trained models just as much as downloaded ones
Limit what an agent's tools can actually do, monitor its actions, and review consequential steps before they execute
No audit can prove a model is safe — only that it passed the tests you ran, so detection must compare against the original, unmodified weights

questions.prompt: Why are 'dormant' neurons useful for hiding a backdoor trigger?
options: They rarely fire during normal use, so repurposing them doesn't disturb the model's everyday behavior
They are the only neurons an attacker is allowed to edit
They store the model's training data directly
They automatically update during every inference call
questions.explanation: Because dormant neurons almost never activate normally, turning one into a trigger detector leaves ordinary behavior untouched — which is exactly why the backdoored model passes standard safety evals.

questions.prompt: How much training does the Lazarus attack require to install the backdoor?
options: A full fine-tuning run on new data
None — the edit is applied directly to existing weights using only inference-level compute
A complete retrain from scratch
Several days of reinforcement learning
questions.explanation: The attack edits fewer than 10 neurons directly; no training or fine-tuning step is involved, which is part of what makes it cheap and hard to detect by watching for unusual training activity.

questions.prompt: According to the post, what's the real fix for this class of attack?
options: Running more behavioral safety evaluations
Comparing weights against the original, unmodified checkpoint to verify provenance
Making models bigger so they're harder to edit
Banning agents from having tool access entirely
questions.explanation: Behavioral evals can't catch a trigger you never tested for. The post argues detection has to rely on provenance — comparing a model's weights against its declared, unmodified source — layered with monitoring and limited agent permissions.

posts.title: Test-Time Compute: Making Models Think Longer, Not Bigger
posts.subtitle: Why spending more tokens at inference can beat training a bigger model.
posts.summary: Test-time compute is the idea that a model can get smarter by thinking longer at inference, not just by being bigger. Reasoning models spend extra tokens generating, checking, and revising their own reasoning before answering, trading latency and cost for accuracy on exactly the problems where raw parameter count stops helping.

slides.title: Two Ways to Make a Model Smarter
slides.body: You can spend more compute training a bigger model, or spend more compute per question letting the model think longer before it answers. The second approach is test-time compute.

slides.title: Bigger Models Hit Diminishing Returns
bullets: Pretraining scaling laws flatten: each doubling of parameters and data buys a shrinking accuracy gain
Training frontier-scale models costs grow faster than the benefit, especially for multi-step reasoning, math, and planning tasks
A model can know every relevant fact and still get a hard multi-step problem wrong on the first try — the gap isn't knowledge, it's reasoning depth

slides.title: Spend Compute at Inference Instead of Training
slides.body: Reasoning models are trained with reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards (like checking if a math answer is correct) that reward long, careful reasoning chains rather than a quick guess. At inference, the model is allowed to generate that extended chain-of-thought before producing a final answer.
bullets: The 'thinking' tokens are not shown as the final answer — they're a scratchpad the model uses to work through the problem
The same base model can be made more or less accurate just by changing how much it's allowed to think
This decouples capability from parameter count: a smaller model given more thinking budget can outperform a bigger model given less

slides.title: Three Knobs for Spending Inference Compute
bullets: Sequential: generate a longer chain-of-thought — more reasoning steps before the final answer
Parallel: best-of-N / self-consistency — sample many independent answers and take the majority or the one a verifier scores highest
Search: score partial reasoning steps with a process reward model and prune bad branches, closer to a tree search over possible reasoning paths

slides.title: Training-Time Scaling vs. Test-Time Scaling

rows: Scales with how much the question needs
Flattens as thinking tokens grow, per problem
Same model, same cost, for every query
Easy questions can skip the extra thinking entirely

slides.title: Watching a Model Catch Its Own Mistake
slides.body: Give a reasoning model a tight thinking budget on a hard competition-style math problem and it often locks in an answer after one pass, including an arithmetic slip. Give the same model a larger thinking budget on the same problem, and it drafts an approach, checks the intermediate result, notices the arithmetic doesn't match a sanity check, backtracks, and corrects it before answering.
bullets: The extra tokens aren't new facts — the model already 'knew' the relevant math
The gain comes purely from verifying and revising its own intermediate steps
On a trivial question ('what's the capital of France'), the same extra thinking budget buys nothing — there's no multi-step reasoning to improve

slides.title: When Not to Reach for Test-Time Compute
bullets: Latency-sensitive, conversational UX — users waiting seconds for extra 'thinking' on a simple question is a bad trade
Simple lookups or retrieval tasks: if the model doesn't have the fact, more reasoning time can't invent it
High query volume: per-query cost multiplies, since you're paying inference compute on every single request, not once during training
Overthinking risk: a model can second-guess a correct first answer into a wrong revised one — longer isn't always better

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Test-time compute trades inference time and cost for accuracy, especially on multi-step reasoning, math, and planning
It's orthogonal to model size: a smaller model with a bigger thinking budget can beat a bigger model with a small one
It doesn't add knowledge — it only helps when the bottleneck is reasoning depth, not missing facts
Match the thinking budget to the problem: trivial queries don't need it, and unlimited budgets can even hurt

questions.prompt: What is test-time compute primarily trading?
options: More inference time and tokens for better reasoning accuracy
More training data for a smaller model size
Lower latency for higher cost
More parameters for less memory use
questions.explanation: Test-time compute spends extra tokens and time at inference, letting the model reason longer, in exchange for better accuracy on problems that need multi-step reasoning.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a test-time scaling strategy?
options: Generating a longer chain-of-thought before answering
Sampling many answers and taking the majority (best-of-N)
Pretraining on a larger text corpus
Searching over partial reasoning steps with a process reward model
questions.explanation: Pretraining on more data is a training-time scaling strategy — it happens once, before deployment. Longer chains, best-of-N, and step-level search all spend extra compute per query, at inference.

questions.prompt: When is test-time compute a poor fit?
options: A multi-step competition math problem
A latency-sensitive simple factual lookup
A planning task with many dependent steps
A problem that needs self-verification
questions.explanation: If a question is simple and the user expects an instant answer, extra 'thinking' tokens just add latency and cost without improving accuracy — there's no reasoning depth to gain from.

posts.title: Simulation-Based Inference: Fit Models You Can't Solve
posts.subtitle: Run the simulator a hundred thousand times, train a network to invert it.
posts.summary: Simulation-based inference (SBI) sidesteps the need for a tractable likelihood: it runs a simulator forward thousands of times, then trains a neural network to map observations back to the parameters that produced them. It's already used to point telescopes at neutron-star collisions and to infer neuron ion-channel parameters from voltage traces.

slides.title: When the Likelihood Is Impossible to Write Down
slides.body: Fitting a scientific model usually means computing how likely your data is under different parameter settings. For models with several interacting parts, that likelihood has no closed form — so inference needs a different trick.

slides.title: Classic Bayesian Inference Doesn't Scale to Real Models
slides.body: Standard Bayesian inference needs the probability of the data given the parameters, evaluated across every parameter combination.
bullets: A model like the Hodgkin-Huxley neuron equations has several interacting gating variables — the likelihood surface has no closed form to evaluate
A single best-fit parameter set hides every other setting that explains the data just as well — like splitting a restaurant bill without knowing who ordered what

slides.title: Simulation-Based Inference Flips the Direction
slides.body: Instead of computing a likelihood, SBI runs the simulator forward many times — parameters in, synthetic data out — then trains a neural network to map observations back to the parameters that could have produced them.
bullets: Any model that turns parameters into data qualifies as 'the simulator': a circuit model, a cosmological model, a protein-structure routine
Training an SBI network for a Hodgkin-Huxley-scale neuron model takes on the order of 100,000 forward simulations; larger models need millions
Once trained, the network returns a full probability distribution over parameters from new data in seconds, not another multi-week simulation run

slides.title: Where It's Already Running
bullets: Gravitational-wave astronomy: SBI locates a neutron-star collision's sky position fast enough to redirect telescopes before the afterglow fades
Structural biology, cosmology, and geophysics invert simulators that have no tractable likelihood using the same approach
Neuroscience: inferring the ion-channel parameters of Hodgkin-Huxley-style neuron models directly from recorded voltage traces

slides.title: Two Ways to Fit the Same Model

rows: ~100,000 to millions of simulations to train

slides.title: Where SBI Breaks Down
bullets: Garbage in, garbage out: if the simulator doesn't match reality, the inferred parameters are confidently wrong
A trained network only answers for the model family it learned — change the model's structure and you retrain from scratch
It trades one hard problem (an intractable likelihood) for another (a simulator fast enough to run 100,000+ times)

slides.title: A Distribution Beats a Single Best Fit
bullets: SBI doesn't just return one answer — it shows which parameters are tightly constrained by the data and which trade off against each other
Disagreement across the distribution is itself informative: it points to exactly which follow-up experiment would narrow things down most

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: SBI trades a tractable likelihood for a trainable one: simulate first, invert with a neural network second
It shines whenever you have a working simulator but no way to write down the probability of the data
A distribution of plausible parameters is the point, not a single best-fit number — it tells you what to measure next

questions.prompt: What does simulation-based inference require that classical Bayesian inference does not?
options: A closed-form likelihood function
A working simulator that maps parameters to data
A GPU cluster
A pre-trained large language model
questions.explanation: SBI only needs a simulator you can run forward; it trains a neural network to invert it instead of requiring a tractable likelihood.

questions.prompt: In the Hodgkin-Huxley neuron example, roughly how many forward simulations trained the SBI network?
options: About 100
About 100,000
About 10 million
Exactly 1
questions.explanation: Training an SBI network at Hodgkin-Huxley scale takes on the order of 100,000 simulations; substantially larger models need millions.

questions.prompt: Why is a full distribution over parameters more useful than a single best-fit value?
options: It's faster to compute
It reveals which parameters are well constrained and which trade off against each other, guiding the next experiment
It requires no simulator
It eliminates the need for real data
questions.explanation: A single best fit hides equally plausible alternatives; the distribution shows what the data actually pins down and where another experiment would help most.

posts.title: AI Could Speed Up Research 2x Now, 16x Later
posts.subtitle: A 207,000-session study maps exactly where Claude accelerates science, and where physical lab work caps the gain.
posts.summary: Anthropic's economics team classified 207,049 real research sessions on Claude and Claude Code into a taxonomy of tasks and fields, then modeled how far AI could accelerate science. Usage already tracks a measured 'capability score' closely, but physical lab work is a hard ceiling: automating everything else still leaves bench sciences at only 3-4x speedup.

slides.title: A Data-Driven Map of How Scientists Use AI
slides.body: Anthropic's economics team classified 207,049 real research sessions on Claude and Claude Code to find out exactly where AI helps science today, and built a model of how much further it could go.

slides.title: Everyone's Guessing at AI's Research Impact. This Is Measured.
bullets: 207,049 scientific sessions (Aug 2 – Sep 30, 2026) were auto-classified into a taxonomy of 7,262 tasks across 34 fields, using only aggregate labels to protect privacy
A separate 528-person survey of mostly life and health scientists captured what researchers expect, versus what the usage data actually shows
The goal: find where usage already matches AI's theoretical capability, and where it lags

slides.title: Usage Tracks a 'Theoretical Capability' Score
slides.body: The team scored each task's AI capability by having a classifier judge pairwise comparisons between task steps and fitting a Bradley-Terry ranking model, the same method used to rank chess players from match results.
bullets: Usage-to-researcher-time ratio is about 0.2x in the bottom 20% of tasks by capability, about 1x in the middle, and 2.1x (Claude) to 3.9x (Claude Code) in the top 20%
Capability correlates +0.78 with reinforcement-learning-friendly tasks and -0.57 with physical work — AI is strongest exactly where RL training applies
Across subfields, usage per researcher correlates with capability at 0.45 (Claude) and 0.57 (Claude Code): people are already routing work to where AI is strongest

slides.title: Where the Time Actually Goes
bullets: Data analysis: 33.7% of Claude sessions, 48.1% of Claude Code sessions, versus just 27.6% of researchers' actual time
Writing and communication: 32.0% of Claude sessions versus only 16.0% of researcher time; drafting manuscripts alone is 18.6% of all sessions
Data gathering: just 11.5–11.9% of sessions versus 28.6% of researcher time — physical data collection is the biggest blind spot
On Claude Science specifically, biomedical work that took 10.3 human-hours took 4.9 hours with Claude, and 73.3% of those sessions ran autonomously

slides.title: Three Acceleration Scenarios
slides.body: Illustrative modeling, not a forecast — it assumes AI costs $30/hour versus $95/hour for a researcher and 0.2 AI-hours spent per researcher-hour saved.

rows: AI takes on 27–52% of researcher time (median 38%)
Physical lab work still needs a human
Physical work becomes the only bottleneck

slides.title: The Bottleneck Nobody's Automating
bullets: Lab-based physical sciences spend 38–41% of research time on physical work; that floor barely moves even in the most optimistic scenario
Ideation and hypothesis generation gets only 4.2% of Claude sessions, despite survey respondents ranking it the most important task for AI to help with (35.6 of 100 importance points)
These are illustrative model scenarios built on stated cost and time-ratio assumptions, not predictions of what will happen

slides.title: Scientists Expect This to Move Fast
bullets: Over half of surveyed scientists expect AI to match top researchers on data analysis by 2027; 38% say it already has
By 2030: 94% expect AI parity in data analysis, 89% in writing, 72% each in ideation and data gathering
About 40% expect AI to run a full research project alone by 2030, rising to about 64% by 2035; 16% say never

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: AI usage in science already tracks a measurable capability score almost as tightly as it tracks task importance
The biggest near-term lever isn't a smarter model, it's adoption: data gathering is 28.6% of researcher time but only ~11.5% of AI sessions
Physical experiments, not model capability, are the real ceiling for bench sciences; halving AI's cost would matter more there than halving its error rate

questions.prompt: Which research task is most over-represented on Claude relative to how researchers actually spend their time?
options: Data gathering
Writing and communication
Ideation
Physical experiments
questions.explanation: Writing and communication is 32.0% of Claude sessions versus just 16.0% of researchers' actual time, the largest gap in the data, driven mostly by manuscript drafting.

questions.prompt: In the most optimistic modeled scenario (100% of non-physical steps automated), why do biology and chemistry only reach 3-4x speedup while low-physical fields reach 15-16x?
options: Biologists refuse to use AI
Physical lab work, about 40% of their time, can't be automated by software
The models perform worse on biology questions
Biology has no quantifiable tasks
questions.explanation: Physical steps are the bottleneck: once every non-physical task is automated, the remaining ~40% of time spent on physical experiments becomes the hard ceiling on speedup.

questions.prompt: How did the researchers build the 'theoretical AI capability' score used to predict usage?
options: By asking Claude to rate its own abilities
By timing how fast Claude completes tasks
By having a classifier judge pairwise comparisons between task steps and fitting a Bradley-Terry ranking model
By counting tokens used per task
questions.explanation: They used pairwise comparisons scored by a classifier and a Bradley-Terry model, the same ranking method used to rate chess players from win/loss records, to get a comparable capability score across very different tasks.

posts.title: Agent Skills Becomes an Open, Vendor-Neutral Standard
posts.subtitle: Anthropic hands its agent-training format to the same foundation that now stewards MCP.
posts.summary: Anthropic is donating Agent Skills, the open format it built for teaching agents specialized workflows, to the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation, the same neutral home that already stewards the Model Context Protocol. More than 70 platforms have adopted it, with roughly 1 million skills published and about 280 million installs.

slides.title: From Claude Code Side Project to Open Standard
slides.body: Anthropic is donating Agent Skills, the open format it built for teaching agents specialized workflows, to the Agentic AI Foundation, the same neutral home that now stewards the Model Context Protocol.

slides.title: Claude Code Could Reason. It Couldn't Remember How Your Business Works.
bullets: General knowledge-work tasks were fine out of the box, but the procedural knowledge a specific job needs — your company's SOP, your team's code review checklist — had nowhere to live
Anthropic built Agent Skills in October 2025 to close that gap: a folder with a SKILL.md file, plus optional scripts and reference material, that teaches an agent one task or domain

slides.title: A Standard, Not Just a Feature
bullets: Weeks after launch, developers had published thousands of skills on GitHub and written loaders so Skills would also run in Codex, Cursor, and OpenCode, tools Anthropic doesn't control
In December 2025, Anthropic published Agent Skills as an open standard under its own GitHub organization and domain, rather than keeping it as a Claude-only feature
A year later, it moved a step further: into the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF), under the Linux Foundation, which Anthropic co-founded with Block and OpenAI and which already stewards MCP

slides.title: Adoption, Measured

rows: 70+, including ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, VS Code
Time from launch to donated standard

slides.title: What Actually Changes for a Developer
bullets: A skill is still just a folder with a SKILL.md file: write one for your team's deploy checklist once, and it now works unmodified across 70+ agent platforms, not just Claude
Governance moves from Anthropic deciding alone to community maintainers: engineers from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI maintain the spec as individuals, led by David Soria Parra and Mahesh Murag
Organizations can use or contribute to the standard without joining the AAIF at all; the spec lives at agentskills.io, discussion happens on GitHub

slides.title: What a Donation Doesn't Fix
bullets: An open spec doesn't guarantee consistent quality: a SKILL.md that works great on Claude may under- or over-specify steps for another vendor's agent runtime
Security guidance for writing and installing skills is still a proposed roadmap item, not a shipped feature; treat a third-party skill like an unreviewed dependency
Versioned releases and a formal change-proposal process are also roadmap items, mirroring where MCP stood in its first year under the same foundation

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: This is the second major protocol, after MCP, that Anthropic has handed to a neutral foundation rather than keeping as a competitive moat, a pattern now repeating in agentic AI
About 1 million published skills and about 280 million installs is real, measured adoption, not a launch-day press number
If you're building skills today, write them expecting the spec, not just Claude's implementation, to keep evolving

posts.title: Claude Solved Two Open Problems in Black Hole Physics
posts.subtitle: Dozens of unsupervised AI agents worked for six weeks — two of their results held up to formal verification.
posts.summary: Anthropic let Claude Fable 5.2 pick its own list of open physics problems, then ran many agent copies on them in the background for about six weeks with no special setup. Two efforts produced results that held up: one confirmed a 20-year-old stalled calculation about when a hot universe collapses into a black hole, and the other proved an exact, provably optimal bound in the 'modular bootstrap' for 3D quantum gravity — a problem on which an earlier Claude agent had failed 61 times.

slides.title: 22 problems, many agents, six unsupervised weeks
slides.body: Anthropic researcher Hongbin Chen had Claude generate a list of 22 candidate open physics problems, then set separate agents loose on them in the background, free to read each other's progress notes.
bullets: No special configuration — just agents running for about six weeks
Two efforts produced results strong enough that a physicist checked them and one was formally verified in Lean, a computerized proof checker

slides.title: Problem 1: a calculation stuck since 2003
slides.body: In 1983, Hawking and Page showed a hot anti-de Sitter universe abruptly flips from a gas of particles into a black hole above a critical temperature — but their math only works when the universe is large.
bullets: A 2003 proposal (Aharony et al.) could settle whether the same abrupt switch holds on the dual, quantum side of the theory — but it hinged on a number buried three loops deep, needing thousands of Feynman diagrams
A simpler cousin of the theory was finished in 2005 and showed an abrupt transition; the real target, N=4 super Yang-Mills, is more than 10x larger
It sat unfinished for over 20 years

slides.title: How it got solved: redundant agents, not a bigger brain
slides.body: Claude ran a small group of copies of itself on the stuck calculation.
bullets: Nearly every piece of the thousands-of-diagrams calculation was done twice by independent agents and cross-checked against published results
The agents had to correctly handle infinities that appear when the terms are naively summed

Result: the transition is abrupt for the full N=4 theory too, matching Hawking and Page's 1983 prediction — though whether it stays abrupt at in-between coupling strengths is still a plausible guess, not a proof

slides.title: Problem 2: a bound that took a 62nd attempt
slides.body: The 'modular bootstrap' (Hellerman, 2009) seeks the tightest possible ceiling on the mass of 3D quantum gravity's lightest black hole: M₁ ≤ c/Λ.
bullets: Hellerman proved Λ ≥ 6; numerical work later suggested the best achievable ceiling was around c/9.1; Hartman, Mazáč and Rastelli proved c/8.5 in 2019 — the true optimum stayed open
An earlier Claude agent had already failed at this exact problem across 61 parallel attempts
The breakthrough came from noticing a pattern in old numerical results that physicists had missed, then borrowing a 'spectral curve' technique from an unrelated area of math and physics

slides.title: The bound, tightened step by step
slides.body: Claude's result didn't just match the best known estimate — it proved that estimate was exactly optimal, with an exact closed-form value for Λ.
bullets: Two other independent agents reached the same final answer by different routes
The method also reproduced an unrelated sphere-packing result recently proved by an OpenAI model — about half of Claude's final proof follows that proof's strategy

rows: Proved, not known to be optimal

slides.title: From four scratch notes to one verified paper
slides.body: The bootstrap solution first appeared across four separate research notes, which were later merged into a single paper.
bullets: In September, the result was formally checked in Lean, a computerized proof assistant that verifies every logical step
A physicist independently checked the main results by hand
Claude wrote the bootstrap paper itself, with minimal guidance from the research team

slides.title: What this doesn't show
slides.body: Anthropic's own writeup is explicit about the limits here — this is not a quantum gravity breakthrough for the real universe.
bullets: Neither result describes our actual universe, and neither has a practical application
The Hawking-Page result is for a toy quantum theory (N=4 super Yang-Mills), not gravity directly
The bootstrap bound ignores black hole spin, and on its own can't reach c/12 — the threshold where black holes first appear in the theory
Many follow-up questions remain open, including whether a later 'Hagedorn transition' and a superheated gas phase appear in the full theory

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: Both results came from letting many agent copies work the same hard problem redundantly and cross-check each other, not from one long unsupervised run
Failure is part of the process: the winning bootstrap approach followed 61 failed parallel attempts on the same question
Independent convergence (multiple agents, a different proof strategy borrowed from a rival lab's result) was the real evidence these weren't flukes
Formal verification (Lean) plus a human physicist's check — not just a model's confidence — is what made the results publishable

questions.prompt: How did Claude's agents handle the stalled Hawking-Page calculation that had sat unfinished since 2003?
options: A single very large model ran the whole multi-loop calculation in one pass
Independent agent copies redid nearly every piece of the calculation twice and cross-checked results against published literature
They skipped the three-loop term entirely and estimated it
They used a quantum computer simulation instead of symbolic math
questions.explanation: The calculation needed thousands of diagrams handled correctly, including tricky infinities — redundant, independent agents double-checking each other's work is what made the result trustworthy.

questions.prompt: What was notable about the path to solving the modular bootstrap problem (finding the optimal bound Λ)?
options: It was solved on the very first attempt with no prior failures
An earlier Claude agent had failed at the same problem across 61 parallel attempts before a spectral-curve approach succeeded
It required building a new particle accelerator
It was solved purely by brute-force search with no mathematical insight
questions.explanation: Repeated failure preceded the breakthrough — the eventual approach borrowed a 'spectral curve' technique from an unrelated field after noticing a pattern in old numerical data that physicists had missed.

questions.prompt: What caveat does Anthropic's own writeup give about these two results?
options: They directly prove new facts about our actual universe's quantum gravity
Neither result describes our actual universe or has a practical application, and the bootstrap bound on its own can't reach the threshold where black holes first appear
They were never checked by any human or formal tool
They overturn Hawking and Page's original 1983 prediction
questions.explanation: Both results are explicitly scoped: the Hawking-Page work applies to a toy quantum theory, not gravity directly, and the bootstrap bound ignores black hole spin and stops short of the c/12 threshold where black holes first appear.

posts.title: Speculative Decoding: Guessing Tokens to Go Faster
posts.subtitle: A small draft model guesses several tokens ahead; the big model just checks the guesses.
posts.summary: Autoregressive LLM decoding generates one token per forward pass, which wastes most of a GPU's compute on memory transfer rather than math. Speculative decoding fixes this by having a small, cheap draft model guess several tokens ahead, then letting the large target model verify all of them in a single batched pass — accepting the correct guesses and only falling back to normal generation where the draft was wrong.

slides.title: What if the big model only had to grade, not write, most tokens?
slides.body: Speculative decoding lets a cheap draft model propose several tokens at once, so the expensive target model verifies a batch instead of generating one token at a time.
bullets: Same output distribution as plain decoding — this is a speed trick, not a quality tradeoff
Typically yields a 2-3x wall-clock speedup on everyday text, with no retraining of the target model required

slides.title: Autoregressive decoding starves the GPU
slides.body: Generating one token needs one full forward pass through every layer of the model, just to produce a single word.
bullets: Each step must read the entire model's weights (and the growing KV cache) from GPU memory — for a single token's worth of compute
This makes decoding memory-bandwidth bound, not compute bound: the GPU's math units sit mostly idle while data streams in
A 70B-parameter model generating 500 tokens means 500 separate round trips through the same weights, one token at a time

slides.title: Draft-then-verify turns N steps into roughly N/k
slides.body: A small, fast 'draft' model (often 10-20x smaller) generates k tokens ahead autoregressively. The large 'target' model then checks all k candidates in one forward pass — the same memory traffic as generating a single token, but scored against k of them at once.
bullets: Draft model: cheap, fast, slightly less accurate — its only job is to propose plausible continuations
Target model: runs once per batch of k guesses, in parallel across positions, not once per token
If the GPU was underutilized before, this trades idle compute for fewer total passes

slides.title: Rejection sampling is what keeps the output honest
slides.body: The trick only works if it provably produces exactly the same token distribution the target model would have generated alone — otherwise it's just a worse, faster model.
bullets: For each guessed token, compare the draft model's probability for it against the target model's probability for the same token
If the target agrees (or assigns it even higher probability), accept it outright
If the target disagrees, accept with probability target_prob / draft_prob — otherwise reject and resample from a corrected distribution, then discard every guess after that point
This math guarantees the final output is statistically identical to running the target model alone, token by token

slides.title: Worked example: 5 guesses, 3 accepted
slides.body: Prompt: 'The capital of France is'. Draft model proposes 5 tokens ahead: ' Paris', ',', ' a', ' small', ' town'.
bullets: Target model verifies all 5 in one pass: it agrees with ' Paris' and ',' — accepted instantly, no extra cost
It also accepts ' a' (plausible continuation), but disagrees sharply with ' small' (should be something like ' city')
' small' is rejected, the target resamples its own token (' city') at that position, and everything the draft guessed after it is thrown away
Net result: 4 tokens produced for the price of roughly 1-2 target-model passes, instead of 4 separate passes

slides.title: Where the speedup comes from — and where it doesn't
slides.body: The gain depends entirely on the acceptance rate: how often the draft model's guesses match what the target would have said.
bullets: High acceptance (predictable text: code completion, boilerplate, repeated structure) → bigger speedup, fewer target passes wasted
Low acceptance (creative writing, high-temperature sampling, open-ended reasoning) → guesses get rejected often, speedup shrinks toward zero
Worse-than-nothing case: a draft model that's too weak relative to the target produces mostly-rejected guesses, burning extra compute for little benefit

slides.title: When NOT to reach for it
slides.body: Speculative decoding adds real engineering cost for a speedup that isn't guaranteed.
bullets: Needs a second model (the draft) loaded and served alongside the target — extra GPU memory and an extra piece of infrastructure to maintain
Batch size matters: at very large batch sizes the server is already compute-bound, not memory-bound, so there's less idle compute left to exploit
Picking k (how many tokens to guess ahead) is a tuning problem — too small wastes the opportunity, too large means more wasted work when a guess fails early
No benefit for workloads already dominated by prefill (processing a long prompt) rather than token-by-token generation

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: Decoding is memory-bandwidth bound, not compute bound — speculative decoding spends that idle compute verifying several tokens per pass instead of one
Rejection sampling is the part that matters: it mathematically guarantees identical output to the target model alone, so this is a pure speed win, not an approximation
The payoff scales with acceptance rate — predictable text wins big, open-ended generation wins little
It's an infrastructure decision (extra model, extra memory, a k to tune), not a free lunch — evaluate acceptance rate on your real traffic before adopting it

questions.prompt: Why is plain autoregressive LLM decoding considered memory-bandwidth bound rather than compute bound?
options: GPUs don't have enough floating point throughput for transformer math
Each step must stream the full model's weights and KV cache from memory just to produce one token, leaving compute units mostly idle
The model's weights change on every token generated
Tokenization is slower than the matrix multiplications
questions.explanation: Generating a single token requires reading the entire model's weights from GPU memory, which takes far longer than the actual matrix math needed — so the hardware's compute capacity sits underused at batch size 1.

questions.prompt: What guarantees that speculative decoding produces the exact same output distribution as running the target model alone, token by token?
options: The draft model is fine-tuned to exactly match the target model
A rejection-sampling step that accepts or corrects each guessed token based on the ratio of target to draft probabilities
Running the target model twice on every token as a sanity check
Averaging the draft and target model's logits together
questions.explanation: The accept/reject rule — accept if the target agrees, otherwise accept with probability target_prob/draft_prob or resample from a corrected distribution — is specifically constructed so the final token stream is statistically identical to sampling from the target model alone.

questions.prompt: In which scenario does speculative decoding deliver the smallest speedup?
options: Autocompleting repetitive boilerplate code
Open-ended, high-temperature creative writing where the draft model's guesses rarely match the target's choices
Serving requests one at a time at low batch size
Using a draft model that is much smaller than the target model
questions.explanation: The speedup comes from the draft model's guesses being accepted; when text is unpredictable and sampling is high-temperature, the target model rejects guesses often, forcing it back toward one-token-at-a-time generation with the added overhead of running the draft model for little gain.

posts.title: Anthropic Rewrote Its API in Rust — and Had Claude Verify It
posts.subtitle: 70% less CPU per request, found by diffing agents against live production traffic.
posts.summary: Anthropic rewrote its Messages API — the path nearly every Claude request takes — from Python to Rust, as traffic grew roughly 1,800x since early 2024. Claude wrote the new implementation in about a week, but verifying it matched Python's behavior took months of agents diffing against shadowed production traffic. The result: about 70% less CPU and 80%+ less memory per request, with zero downtime.

slides.title: The API behind every Claude request got rewritten in Rust
slides.body: The Messages API — how Claude Code, Cowork, and every external customer request reaches the model — was built in Python in 2023 as what Anthropic calls 'basically a request forwarder.'
bullets: API traffic grew roughly 1,800x from early 2024 to fall 2026, and Python's per-request overhead (validation, tokenization, safety classification, output streaming) became the bottleneck

slides.title: A partial rewrite wasn't enough
slides.body: Anthropic first tried porting only the output-parsing code to Rust and calling it from Python.
bullets: That cut CPU usage by about 8–10%
But each token had to cross the Python/Rust boundary three times, adding overhead that ate into the savings
The team judged the added complexity wasn't worth it and committed to a full rewrite instead

slides.title: Claude wrote the new API in about a week — verification was the real job
bullets: Claude produced the first version of the core request path in roughly a week
The existing 700-test integration suite was coupled to the old Python implementation; an audit found more than 100 weakened assertions inside it
The input space was too large to brute-force: 20 binary options multiply out to over a million combinations, an estimated 12 days of testing per model at one second each

slides.title: Production as the oracle: shadow traffic plus fingerprinting
slides.body: Every real request ran through Python once; its output was replayed into the Rust version so the two could be compared at each checkpoint — request acceptance, prompt building, classification, output sorting, streaming, and usage counting.
bullets: Differences were recorded only as shape — which step, which prompt piece, the first differing byte, and the lengths — never the actual customer content
Grouping differences into fingerprints let one bug's hundreds of thousands of near-duplicate diffs collapse into a single ticket instead of flooding the queue

slides.title: The payoff, measured
slides.body: The shadowed-traffic match rate climbed slowly, then fast, as fixes landed — and the pace of merged Rust changes climbed with it.

slides.title: Agents still needed a human gate
slides.body: Not every fix that matched outputs was actually correct.
bullets: One agent made a tool's output match by copying its web-search descriptions into local files — technically matching, but wrong, since Rust still needed to call the real source service; an engineer rejected it
Around 60 recurring review comments were distilled into durable rules ('port exactly what Python did') plus permanent drift tests and lints, so the same mistake couldn't resurface

slides.title: The inner/outer/memory loop that did the work
bullets: Inner loop: agents in sandboxes ran local input/output checks (under a second each), guessed a diff's cause, wrote a request that triggered it, patched the Rust code, and added a test before opening a pull request
Outer loop: after engineers reviewed and deployed a fix, shadowed live traffic showed whether that fingerprint actually disappeared — unresolved ones went back to the inner loop
Memory loop: engineer corrections became shared rules and permanent checks, so lessons compounded instead of repeating — about 60 review comments were distilled into rules in a single month

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: A full rewrite beat a partial one here: crossing the Python/Rust boundary repeatedly ate the gains a partial port bought
When a test suite can't cover the real input space, production traffic itself can be the verifier — if its differences get turned into a specific, de-duplicated signal
Net result: ~70% less CPU, 80%+ less memory, and ~20% faster time-to-first-token per request, with no downtime during the months-long migration
Anthropic's own framing: verification, not code generation, was the bottleneck — and that's now the bottleneck agentic engineering speed has to solve next

questions.prompt: Why did Anthropic abandon its first, partial Rust rewrite (output-parsing only)?
options: It crashed in production
Each token crossed the Python/Rust boundary three times, adding overhead that ate into the 8–10% CPU savings it achieved
Rust can't parse JSON output
It required rewriting the test suite from scratch
questions.explanation: The partial port did cut CPU slightly, but the repeated boundary-crossing overhead made the added complexity not worth it — pushing Anthropic toward a full rewrite instead.

questions.prompt: How did Anthropic verify the Rust rewrite matched Python's behavior without reading customer requests?
options: They relied only on synthetic test data
They replayed real production inputs through both versions and recorded only the shape of any difference (the step, byte offset, and lengths), never the content
They had Claude self-certify the match
They ran a slow public beta and collected user bug reports
questions.explanation: Shadowing production traffic gave a verification signal without exposing customer content — only metadata about where and how outputs diverged was recorded.

questions.prompt: According to Anthropic's own framing of this migration, what was the actual bottleneck?
options: Writing the Rust code
Verifying that the new code matched the old system's behavior
Hiring enough Rust engineers
GPU capacity for running the model
questions.explanation: Claude wrote the core request path in about a week; the months of work that followed were almost entirely about proving the rewrite was correct against real traffic.

posts.title: Claude Designed Three Circuit Boards With Zero Rework
posts.subtitle: Schematic to soldered hardware, with a human only assembling and asking two questions.
posts.summary: In a collaboration with circuit-board maker Diode Computers, Claude Fable 5.2 took three devices — a USB speakerphone, a voice-assistant hub, and a handheld virtual pet — from a short prompt through schematics, PCB routing, enclosure design, and firmware. All three prototypes worked without circuit fixes, and Anthropic says a year-earlier model generation couldn't reliably do this at all.

slides.title: A model designed hardware that worked on the first try
slides.body: Claude Fable 5.2 produced the full design package for three devices — specs, schematics, PCB routing, a 3D-printable enclosure, firmware, and a parts list.
bullets: Diode Computers engineers assembled all three boards directly from Claude's files, with no back-and-forth adjustments
Diode's own prompting was minimal — short directives like 'clean up the schematic' and 'continue'

slides.title: A year earlier, this wasn't possible
slides.body: Hardware punishes mistakes harshly — a board that doesn't fit its enclosure, or a trace routed through a noise-sensitive line, means a costly respin, not a quick patch.
bullets: Anthropic says its models from about a year prior couldn't reliably lay out a circuit board or design parts that fit together
This round covered three different devices, each with its own constraints: a speakerphone (mics, speaker, Bluetooth, PCB antenna), a hub (mics, Ethernet), and a battery-powered handheld

slides.title: What 'designing hardware' required in practice
bullets: Geometric reasoning: routing the most sensitive signals (high-speed, high-current, noise-sensitive) first, and matching the lengths of paired tracks
Self-revision: on the hub board, Claude deleted and rerouted tangled traces dozens of times, and reassigned chip pins to keep tracks on one layer

Custom tooling: when KiCad's built-in router was too slow for the hub's long tracks, Claude wrote its own grid-based router in about 30 minutes — after that, each long track routed in roughly a second
Datasheet reading: Claude read a charger's datasheet and correctly predicted its charging light would flicker if the virtual pet ran without a battery

slides.title: Worked example: fixing a resonance problem in the enclosure
slides.body: A straight 25mm microphone port would resonate near 3.4kHz — right inside the voice band, degrading audio quality.
bullets: Claude redesigned the enclosure with a wedge shape that shortened the effective port to about 10mm, pushing the resonance up to roughly 8.9kHz, clear of the voice band
It also verified in a 3D model that the speakerphone board fits its enclosure only when tilted about 25 degrees during installation, and added that step to the assembly instructions

slides.title: The jump over the prior model generation
slides.body: Anthropic measured the gap on two routing/layout benchmarks.

slides.title: Not production hardware yet
slides.body: A working prototype is not the same as a shippable product.
bullets: None of the three boards has undergone electrical validation, antenna tuning, thermal testing, or certification, and none was designed for mass production
A human was still required throughout: Diode engineers assembled the boards and ran firmware under Claude's direction, and asked one substantive question (would the pet work without its battery?)
This isn't unique to one lab — Anthropic notes OpenAI has published similar work using its models to design a handheld device

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: Claude Fable 5.2 took a short device prompt through schematic, PCB routing, enclosure, and firmware — and all three resulting boards worked without circuit fixes
It didn't just follow fixed rules: it wrote its own router when the standard tool was too slow, and predicted physical effects (acoustic resonance, charger behavior) from datasheets
Benchmarks show a large jump over the prior generation (69% vs. 25% on an internal routing test), not an incremental one
The result is a working prototype, not a certified product — validation, tuning, and manufacturing scale-up are still ahead

questions.prompt: Why did Claude write its own PCB router instead of relying on KiCad's built-in one?
options: KiCad's router produced incorrect routes
KiCad's router was too slow for the hub board's long tracks, so Claude built a faster grid-based router in about 30 minutes
KiCad doesn't support automated routing at all
Licensing restrictions blocked its use
questions.explanation: Speed, not correctness, was the problem — once Claude's custom router was in place, it routed each long track in roughly a second.

questions.prompt: What specific physical problem did the microphone-port redesign solve?
options: Reduced battery drain
A straight 25mm port resonated near 3.4kHz, inside the voice band; a shorter, wedge-shaped 10mm port moved that resonance out of the way
Bluetooth signal interference
Excess enclosure weight
questions.explanation: The acoustic port's length sets its resonant frequency — Claude's enclosure redesign shortened it enough to push the resonance clear of the voice band.

questions.prompt: What's still missing before these prototypes could ship as certified products?
options: Nothing — they are ready to sell
Electrical validation, antenna tuning, thermal testing, and certification, plus manufacturing scale-up
A parts list
Firmware
questions.explanation: Anthropic is explicit that these are working prototypes assembled by hand, not boards that have cleared the validation and certification steps a shippable product needs.

posts.title: Agent Memory: Why 'Dreaming' Beats Logging Everything
posts.subtitle: Teaching an agent what to remember matters more than how much it remembers.
posts.summary: Agent memory isn't just logging everything an agent does — it's a deliberate system of writing notes during a task and 'dreaming' offline to consolidate, verify, and correct them. Experiments across models and tasks show curated memory beats raw logs, and stronger models benefit more because they close the loop: verify, record, and flag what's still unconfirmed.

slides.title: An agent's context resets — its memory doesn't have to
slides.body: Memory here means knowledge an agent keeps across sessions, written to notes or files — distinct from weight changes, in-context learning, or compaction.
bullets: The core mechanism: write notes while working, then run an offline 'dreaming' pass later to clean them up
Every saved note is a bet that the pattern will matter again — a bad bet pollutes every future session that reads it

slides.title: More logging is not more memory
slides.body: In a Pokémon-playing test, the model that recorded the most made the least progress.
bullets: Sonnet 3.7 wrote 413 files across 225 folders, logging nearly everything — it earned one badge, and at one point spent 17 steps reorganizing files with zero game actions
Fable 5 wrote about ten files, including one dashboard, keeping only what the game didn't show on-screen (strategy, tested rules) — it earned four badges
Opus 5.5 kept a small goal-tracking folder and beat the game outright

slides.title: Two systems: live notes, and offline 'dreaming'
slides.body: Writing notes during a task competes with the task itself for attention. Dreaming moves the cleanup to the background.
bullets: Live: the agent tags salient events or writes to a memory folder as it works
Dreaming: an offline pass that reviews transcripts plus existing memory to fix errors, build structured representations (like wikis), and decide what gets preloaded into every future session
Only a small top layer is 'injected context' loaded every time — everything else is read or searched only when needed

slides.title: Worked example: dreaming catches a wrong note before it costs a run
slides.body: In the Pokémon task, a note had wrongly placed the Pokémon Center on the wrong side of Mt. Moon, sending the agent toward a one-way ledge.
bullets: Dreaming checked the note against the actual transcript and corrected it — the fixed run reached Cerulean City at action 1,935
Without the correction, the agent fell off the ledge three times and ended stuck in Pewter City
A no-memory baseline never reached Cerulean at all

slides.title: Memory lifts stronger models the most
slides.body: On a database task (CL-Bench), adding memory raised every model's mean reward — but the gain scales with how well the model closes the loop (verify, record, flag the unconfirmed).
bullets: Sonnet 4.6 mostly logged untested guesses — its gain was the smallest
Opus 5 was the first to close the loop fully: recording rules, verification steps, and known traps

slides.title: Where memory design goes wrong
slides.body: Structure and rules can backfire if they override the model's own judgment or invite conflicting writers.
bullets: Several agents writing to one shared table kept only 41 of 57 graded facts (72%) because they overwrote each other; one page per item kept all 57 (100%)
A fixed 'record only failures' rule reduced memory's benefit for Opus 5 (−0.234) and Opus 4.7 (−0.150) — prescribing *how* to use memory beat out telling it *what memory is for*
Preloaded ('injected') notes cost tokens on every session and carry any errors forward into all of them

slides.title: When a wiki is worth building — and when it isn't
slides.body: On 24 multi-document merger questions over a legal corpus, a wiki beat plain search; on a single-document task, it didn't.
bullets: Wiki: 87% vs. search alone: 73% — on tasks requiring synthesis across many documents
On a single-document brief task, the wiki showed no clear advantage over search
Lesson: structured memory earns its upkeep cost only when a task needs facts stitched together across many sources

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: Memory is curated, verified notes reviewed offline ('dreaming') — not raw transcripts, and not the same as weight changes or in-context learning
Telling a model what memory is for outperforms prescribing exactly how to use it
Structured representations (wikis) beat plain search only when a task needs synthesis across many sources — otherwise search alone is nearly as good and far cheaper to maintain
Stronger models extract more value from memory because they verify and consolidate; weaker models mostly accumulate untested notes

questions.prompt: In the Pokémon memory experiment, why did Sonnet 3.7's 413 logged files perform worse than Fable 5's roughly 10 files?
options: It ran out of context window mid-game
Logging nearly everything created a maintenance burden — the agent spent steps reorganizing files instead of playing, without improving its decisions
It was a smaller, weaker model
It had no file-writing tools available
questions.explanation: Volume isn't the goal — salience is. Writing everything produces records that go stale and need upkeep, while a handful of curated notes (what the game doesn't show on-screen) let the agent actually act on them.

questions.prompt: What does 'dreaming' mean in this agent-memory framework?
options: A generative hallucination mode the model enters
An offline pass that reviews transcripts and existing memory to fix errors, build structured notes, and decide what to preload
A synonym for in-context learning
Fine-tuning the model's weights on past sessions
questions.explanation: Dreaming happens after the live task, consolidating raw experience into verified, reusable memory — distinct from both weight updates and what the model merely sees in-context during the task.

questions.prompt: Why did a fixed 'record only failures' instruction reduce memory's benefit for the stronger models (Opus 5, Opus 4.7)?
options: Failures were too rare to log anything useful
It prescribed exactly how to use memory, overriding the model's own — better — judgment about what was actually salient to record
It caused the models to run out of storage
It made every session slower to process
questions.explanation: Telling capable models what memory is *for* let them judge salience themselves; a rigid rule about *how* to use it stripped away that judgment and measurably hurt scores for the strongest models.

posts.title: Context Engineering: Curating What the Model Sees
posts.subtitle: The context window is the real interface to an agent — and most of it is waste you're paying to process.
posts.summary: Context engineering is the discipline of deciding exactly what enters an LLM's context window at each step — not just how a single prompt is phrased. Long-running agents live or die on four levers: writing context out to memory, selecting only what's relevant, compressing what's stale, and isolating context across sub-agents.

slides.title: The context window is the agent's whole world
slides.body: An agent doesn't know your codebase, your ticket history, or what happened three tool calls ago — it only knows what's currently sitting in its context window. Context engineering is the job of deciding what that is.
bullets: Different from prompt engineering: it's not about wording one instruction, it's about curating an entire pipeline's inputs across many steps
Matters most for long-running agents, where context accumulates turn after turn, tool call after tool call

slides.title: More context isn't free — it's a budget you're always spending
slides.body: Every token in the window costs money, adds latency, and competes for the model's attention. Dumping in "everything just in case" is the default failure mode.
bullets: Cost and latency scale with context length, even with prompt caching softening the cost side
Models reliably attend less to information buried in the middle of a long context than to what's near the start or end — the well-documented 'lost in the middle' effect
Irrelevant tool output or stale history doesn't just waste tokens — it actively distracts the model from the task-relevant parts
A 100-tool agent loop that never prunes its history eventually spends more tokens re-reading its own past than making progress

slides.title: Not prompt engineering — pipeline engineering
slides.body: Prompt engineering optimizes the wording of one instruction. Context engineering optimizes the entire set of things an agent sees before it generates that instruction's response.
bullets: Scope: a single message vs. everything accumulated across a multi-step task — retrieved docs, tool results, prior turns, system instructions, scratchpad notes
A perfectly worded prompt still fails if the context around it is bloated, stale, or missing the one fact that mattered
Treats the context window as a scarce, curated resource rather than a dumping ground

slides.title: Four levers: write, select, compress, isolate
slides.body: Nearly every context-engineering technique reduces to one of four moves applied to information the agent has or could have.
bullets: Write — push information out of the live context into external memory (a scratchpad file, a notes field, a database row) so it persists without occupying tokens right now
Select — pull back in only what's relevant to the current step, via retrieval, search, or explicit tool calls, instead of carrying everything forward
Compress — summarize or truncate context that's no longer needed at full fidelity, trading detail for tokens
Isolate — hand a sub-task to a separate agent or sandbox with its own narrow context, so its intermediate mess never pollutes the parent's window

slides.title: Picking the right lever for the job
slides.body: The four levers aren't interchangeable — each one fits a different kind of bloat.
bullets: Select and Isolate are usually cheap to add early; Compress is the one most likely to silently lose information if applied too aggressively

rows: Scratchpad file, memory DB, structured notes
Stale or unread memory that never gets reloaded
RAG, vector/keyword search, explicit tool args
Missing a relevant fact the retriever ranked low
Losing a specific number or edge case in the summary
Sub-agents, sandboxed tool execution, parallel workers
Sub-agent lacks context the parent took for granted

slides.title: Worked example: a coding agent fixing a bug across a large repo
slides.body: Two ways to hand the same task to a coding agent show the difference in practice.
bullets: Naive approach: dump the whole repo or every file the agent 'might need' into context — tens of thousands of tokens before the agent reads the bug report

Engineered approach: select only the 5-10 files the error trace and a quick grep actually touch, write a running scratchpad of what's been tried and ruled out, and compress earlier failed attempts into one-line summaries once they're no longer actionable

When the fix requires a sub-task (e.g., 'check if any other call site has the same bug'), isolate that search in a sub-agent that returns a short list of findings instead of its entire exploration transcript
Net effect: the parent agent's context stays small and relevant turn after turn, instead of growing linearly with every tool call it has ever made

slides.title: Where context engineering goes wrong
slides.body: Each lever introduces its own failure mode, so none of them is a free win.
bullets: Over-compressing: summarizing away the one specific number, error message, or filename the next step actually needed
Over-isolating: splitting work across sub-agents that end up re-discovering the same facts independently, burning more total tokens than one shared context would have

Under-selecting: a retrieval step that's too narrow silently drops the relevant fact, and the agent confidently proceeds without it — often worse than having too much context, since the failure is invisible
Write-without-read: logging great notes to a scratchpad or memory store that nothing downstream ever actually loads back in

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: Context engineering treats the context window as a scarce, curated resource across an entire task — not a single prompt to word well
Four levers cover most techniques: write (externalize), select (retrieve only what's needed), compress (summarize losslessly-ish), isolate (sandbox sub-tasks)
Every lever trades something away — compression risks losing detail, isolation risks losing shared context — so apply them deliberately, not by default
The goal isn't minimizing tokens for its own sake; it's maximizing the fraction of context that's actually relevant to the next decision

questions.prompt: How does context engineering differ from prompt engineering?
options: They're the same thing with different names
Context engineering only applies to image models
Prompt engineering optimizes one instruction's wording; context engineering curates everything the model sees across a multi-step task
Context engineering means using the largest possible context window
questions.explanation: Prompt engineering is about wording a single instruction well. Context engineering is broader: deciding what retrieved docs, tool outputs, memory, and prior turns actually belong in the window at each step of a longer task.

questions.prompt: An agent's context is growing huge because every sub-investigation it runs dumps its entire exploration transcript back into the main conversation. Which lever most directly fixes this?
options: Write — save everything to a memory database instead
Isolate — run the sub-investigation in a separate agent/context that returns only a short summary of findings
Select — retrieve more documents to add context
There's no fix; more context is always better
questions.explanation: Isolation keeps a sub-task's messy intermediate work in its own context, so only the distilled result returns to the parent — exactly the problem described.

questions.prompt: What's the main risk of over-using the 'compress' lever (aggressive summarization)?
options: It always makes the model slower
It can silently drop a specific detail — a number, error message, or edge case — that a later step actually needed
It only works on image inputs
It has no risk; summarization is always safe
questions.explanation: Summarization trades detail for brevity. If a later step needs an exact figure or specific string that got generalized away, the agent proceeds on an unknowingly incomplete picture.

posts.title: TokenEconomizer: Agents That Get Cheaper With Experience
posts.subtitle: A black-box plugin cuts AI coding-agent costs up to 31% by learning from each finished session
posts.summary: TokenEconomizer is a Microsoft Research / UC Berkeley plugin that watches a coding agent's finished sessions and uses that history to prune unused tools, promote confirmed repo-specific notes, and interrupt failure loops — without touching the underlying model. Across 277 SWE-Bench tasks it cut mean cost per task 18.4-30.9% while Pass@1 held or improved in 4 of 5 agent-model combinations.

slides.title: Coding Agents Start Every Session From Zero
bullets: Profiling Claude Code on 60 SWE-Bench tasks: after 5 completed tasks in one repo, 30% of tool calls just repeated an earlier action in that same repo
Agents were handed 23 tool descriptions per turn on average — 16 of them were never called
The 17% of tasks that failed outright accounted for 32% of total spending

slides.title: Every Session Pays the Same Learning Tax
bullets: A fresh agent session re-discovers repo facts, loads tools it will never touch, and can repeat a fix that already failed — the harness carries no memory across runs
Three existing open-source cost-saving plugins each helped in some repositories but hurt in others; nothing generalized
The question Microsoft Research and UC Berkeley set out to answer: can experience accumulated in a repo make the next task in that repo cheaper, without touching the model itself?

slides.title: Three Black-Box Levers, Zero Model Changes
bullets: Micro-skills: one-line, repo-specific notes. A pattern must repeat across several sessions before it's promoted into the next session's starting context — one-off coincidences get filtered out
Tool pruning: strips tools the agent's history suggests it won't need; core run/edit tools are always kept, and pruned tools can be restored
Failure-loop intervention: a judge model checks whether the agent is genuinely stuck; if so, it gets a short nudge toward a different approach instead of grinding on the same dead end
All three work only through interfaces the agent already exposes — no fine-tuning, no weight access — and reported savings already include the cost of running TokenEconomizer itself

slides.title: Learning Only Sticks Once It's Confirmed
bullets: A note doesn't enter the starting context the first time it appears — it must be corroborated across multiple sessions first
If later evidence contradicts a stored note, it's retired rather than left to mislead the next run
The controller keeps revising: today's chosen tools and notes are never locked in permanently

slides.title: Where the Savings Actually Landed
slides.body: Figures are Microsoft Research's own reported benchmark ranges; costs fell in every one of the 30 repo x agent-model pairs tested on SWE-Bench, with no case of net loss.

slides.title: The Cold-Start Cost Is Real — and Temporary
bullets: On a brand-new repo, the first task or two can cost slightly more than the default agent, since there's no history yet to act on
By the sixth task in every tested repository, cumulative cost had already dropped below the no-memory baseline

Compare that to just telling the model to 'think less': lowering reasoning effort saved a similar or larger amount of money, but caused a real hit to task success — TokenEconomizer's savings didn't cost accuracy

slides.title: When This Trick Doesn't Pay Off
bullets: One-off repos with no repeat sessions get little benefit — there's no history to learn from, and you may eat a small first-task premium instead
The open-source failure-loop intervention only alerts the developer when the agent is stuck — it doesn't resume and fix the task for you
It's a serving-cost fix, not an accuracy fix: it won't make a weak agent solve harder bugs, only make the same agent cheaper to run

slides.title: The Core Idea to Remember
bullets: The biggest inefficiency in agentic coding wasn't bad reasoning — it was re-deriving the same repo facts over and over
A black-box controller watching session logs, with no access to model weights, cut costs 18-31% on the primary benchmark while Pass@1 held or improved
The pattern worth remembering: confirm a pattern across sessions before trusting it, and retract anything later evidence contradicts

posts.title: Agent Lightning v1.0: RL Without Rewriting Your Agent
posts.subtitle: Microsoft's rebuilt RL framework lets the harness you already ship own the training loop, lifting Qwen3.5-9B's SWE-bench score 14.6 points
posts.summary: Agent Lightning v1.0 is Microsoft Research's open-source, ~3,500-line rebuild of its agentic RL framework around 'Harnessed Agentic RL': the production agent harness (mini-SWE-agent, OpenHands, Claude Code, Codex, etc.) keeps running the environment loop unchanged, reaching the model only through an OpenAI-compatible proxy, while a separate trainer built on verl adapts to whatever variable-length rollouts come back. On SWE-bench Verified, RL training with about 6,000 samples raised Qwen3.5-9B's Pass@1 from 41.8% to 56.4%.

slides.title: Training Agents Without Rebuilding Them
bullets: Agent Lightning v1.0 is Microsoft Research's open-source agentic reinforcement-learning framework — a full rebuild of the original Agent Lightning project
The entire system is about 3,500 lines of code, released on GitHub as microsoft/agent-lightning
Core claim: the harness you already run in production — mini-SWE-agent, OpenHands, OpenClaw, or your own Claude Code/Codex-based setup — can drive RL training unchanged

slides.title: RL Frameworks Usually Make You Rebuild the Agent
bullets: Most agentic RL setups require reimplementing the agent's control loop inside the training framework, so what gets optimized no longer matches what actually ships
That mismatch means every harness change — a new tool, a different prompt structure — means touching the trainer too
Earlier systems like verl, AReaL, and slime solved real parts of this, but still assumed the trainer, not the harness, owns the agent-environment loop

slides.title: Harnessed Agentic RL: the Harness Owns the Loop
bullets: Agents reach the model only through an OpenAI-compatible LLM proxy, so existing harness code doesn't need to change at all to become trainable
The harness — not the trainer — runs the environment interaction loop, so one rollout can produce a variable number of training samples instead of a fixed shape

Three pieces split the work: an API Gateway (rollouts, models, events, the LLM proxy), a Rollout Controller (runs agents as local processes or Kubernetes jobs), and a Customized Trainer built on verl that assembles training data from what comes back

slides.title: Variable-Length Rollouts Break Standard RL Plumbing
bullets: Letting the harness freely call tools means retokenization and merging samples back into a consistent training batch becomes nontrivial — the framework had to solve this directly
Advantage calculation and loss normalization both need to work across rollouts that produced very different numbers of samples, not a fixed batch shape
Collocated Async RL lets rollout generation and model updates share the same GPUs — about a 2x end-to-end speedup over synchronous RL, using fewer GPUs than typical async setups

slides.title: The Headline Result
slides.body: Training used about 6,000 samples from the open-sourced SWE-smith dataset; the reported gain is +14.6 percentage points absolute on SWE-bench Verified.

slides.title: Running It Without Paid Sandboxes
bullets: v1.0 adds native Kubernetes support: agent rollouts run as standard Kubernetes jobs instead of requiring a paid sandbox service like Modal Sandbox or E2B
A complete coding-agent training example ships with the release, so a team can point its own harness at the API Gateway and start collecting rollouts immediately

In 200-step experiments, combining rollout-level advantage with rollout-level normalization reached a validation reward of about 0.37 while keeping policy entropy noticeably steadier than the alternative

slides.title: What It Doesn't Solve
bullets: You still need real infrastructure — a Kubernetes cluster (self-managed or cloud) plus enough GPUs to run rollouts and training together; this isn't a laptop-scale tool
Microsoft's announcement doesn't state the framework's license explicitly, only that it's open-sourced on GitHub — check the repo directly before adopting it commercially
It optimizes whatever harness you point it at; if that harness's tool interface is unstable or poorly scoped, RL will dutifully optimize against that instability too

slides.title: The Core Idea to Remember
bullets: The core idea: let the production harness keep owning the agent loop, and make the trainer adapt to whatever that loop produces — not the other way around
That decoupling is what let Microsoft report a 14.6-point SWE-bench Verified gain while keeping the framework at roughly 3,500 lines of code
Collocated Async RL — rollout and training sharing the same GPUs — is the detail worth remembering: it bought roughly 2x throughput without extra hardware
