posts.title: KV Cache Quantization: Shrink Memory, Not the Model
posts.subtitle: Long-context serving is bottlenecked by the KV cache, not the weights — compressing it buys the context window back
posts.summary: The KV cache stores every past token's key and value vectors so attention doesn't recompute them, but it grows with context length and concurrency until it dwarfs the model's own weights in memory. Quantizing it — INT8 or sub-4-bit instead of FP16, with separate scaling strategies for keys and values — can shrink that footprint 2-4x, letting approaches like KVQuant push a single GPU's usable context into the millions of tokens.

slides.title: The Cache Nobody Budgeted For
bullets: Every token an LLM generates attends over all previous tokens' key and value vectors — so the model caches those vectors (the 'KV cache') instead of recomputing them every step
The KV cache's memory footprint scales with context length x batch size x model depth — at long contexts it can dwarf the memory the weights themselves take up
Quantizing the KV cache — storing those cached numbers in fewer bits — trades almost nothing for a large, direct memory win

slides.title: Weights Are Fixed Size; the Cache Isn't
bullets: A model's weights take a fixed amount of memory no matter what you ask it — a 7B model in FP16 is always about 14GB of weights
The KV cache grows with every token generated and with every concurrent request a server handles, so it's the part of memory usage that actually spirals at serving time

Weight quantization (shrinking the model itself) and KV cache quantization (shrinking what the model remembers about the conversation so far) solve different problems and are typically applied together, not interchangeably

slides.title: Quantize the Numbers That Don't Need Full Precision
bullets: Instead of storing each cached key/value element as FP16 (2 bytes), store it as INT8 or INT4 (1 byte or half a byte) plus a small per-group scale factor used to reconstruct the approximate original value

The scale factor is usually computed per-channel or per small group rather than once for the whole tensor — key/value activations have outlier channels that a single global scale would clip or waste precision on

KVQuant (Hooper et al., 2024) reports sub-4-bit KV cache quantization with under 0.1 perplexity degradation on LLaMA models, by quantizing keys per-channel and values per-token and isolating outlier values into a separate higher-precision store

slides.title: Keys and Values Don't Compress the Same Way
bullets: Key vectors tend to have a few channels with consistently large magnitude across all tokens — quantizing per-channel (one scale per dimension, shared across tokens) handles this well
Value vectors vary more token-to-token rather than channel-to-channel — quantizing per-token (one scale per cached token) tends to work better for them
Using the same quantization scheme for both is a common shortcut that leaves accuracy on the table — this key/value asymmetry is the detail most naive implementations miss

slides.title: What Lower Precision Buys, Byte for Byte
slides.body: Byte counts are definitional (precision x element), not a measured benchmark; KVQuant reports hitting the 4-bit end of this range with under 0.1 perplexity loss on LLaMA models by isolating outliers into a separate higher-precision store.

slides.title: What 4x Smaller Actually Buys You
bullets: Cutting KV cache bytes-per-token 4x means a server can hold roughly 4x the context length per request, or roughly 4x the concurrent requests, in the same GPU memory — whichever the workload needs more
KVQuant's headline claim: LLaMA-7B inference with a 10-million-token context length on a single A100-80GB GPU — a context length that would be impossible at FP16 KV cache on that hardware

This stacks with other serving tricks: PagedAttention solves KV cache fragmentation, continuous batching solves GPU utilization, and KV cache quantization solves raw cache size — production servers typically run all three together

slides.title: Where Quantizing the Cache Bites Back
bullets: Going too aggressive (naive INT4 or lower, no outlier handling) measurably degrades long-context recall and multi-step reasoning before it shows up in simple perplexity numbers — perplexity alone can hide the damage
Per-channel or per-token scale factors add a dequantization step to every attention computation — a real, usually small, compute overhead traded for the memory win
If you're not memory-bound — short contexts, low concurrency, plenty of GPU headroom — KV cache quantization adds complexity and precision risk for a memory saving you don't need yet

slides.title: The Core Idea to Remember
bullets: The KV cache, not the model weights, is usually what runs out of memory first at long context or high concurrency — that's the problem KV cache quantization targets
Keys and values compress asymmetrically: per-channel scaling suits keys' outlier channels, per-token scaling suits values' token-to-token variance
Sub-4-bit KV cache quantization with careful outlier handling has pushed single-GPU context lengths into the millions of tokens — a scale unreachable at FP16
It's a serving-layer lever independent of weight quantization — the two stack, they don't substitute for each other

questions.prompt: What specifically does the KV cache store, and why does it exist?
options: The model's weight matrices, kept in a faster-to-access format
Previously computed key and value vectors for every past token, so attention doesn't recompute them each step
A cache of the most frequent output tokens
A compressed copy of the training dataset
questions.explanation: Attention must compare the current token against every previous token's key and value vectors. Caching those vectors instead of recomputing them is what makes autoregressive generation fast — but it means memory grows with every generated token.

questions.prompt: Why do KV cache quantization schemes often use different scaling strategies for keys versus values?
options: They don't — the same per-tensor scale works equally well for both
Keys tend to have consistent outlier channels across tokens (favoring per-channel scaling), while values vary more token-to-token (favoring per-token scaling)
Values are always stored in full precision regardless of the quantization scheme
Keys are quantized only during training, never during inference
questions.explanation: This asymmetry is a key finding behind approaches like KVQuant: treating keys and values identically leaves accuracy on the table, because their statistical patterns across tokens differ.

questions.prompt: A server never runs out of GPU memory at the context lengths and concurrency it actually serves. What does KV cache quantization offer it?
options: A large, necessary memory win it should always apply
Added complexity and precision risk for a memory saving that workload doesn't currently need
Guaranteed faster token generation with no tradeoffs
A way to increase model accuracy beyond its base performance
questions.explanation: KV cache quantization is a lever for memory-bound serving. If a workload isn't memory-bound, the dequantization overhead and precision risk aren't worth taking on — it solves a specific bottleneck, not a universal one.

posts.title: Mixture of Experts: Scaling Params Without Scaling Compute
posts.subtitle: Sparse routing lets a model hold huge capacity while touching only a sliver of it per token
posts.summary: Mixture of Experts replaces a transformer's single feed-forward block with many smaller expert FFNs plus a learned router that activates only a few per token. That decouples total parameter count from per-token compute, letting models like DeepSeek-V3 hold 671B parameters while spending only ~37B worth of compute on any given token — at the cost of needing every expert resident in memory and a load-balancing problem that doesn't exist in dense models.

slides.title: One Model, Many Specialists
bullets: Dense transformers run every parameter on every token — a 70B model does 70B-parameters worth of math per token, always, easy tokens included
Mixture of Experts (MoE) swaps the feed-forward block for dozens of smaller 'expert' feed-forwards plus a router that picks only a few per token
DeepSeek-V3 holds 671B total parameters but activates only about 37B per token — most of the model sits idle for any single piece of text

slides.title: Dense Scaling Ties Compute to Capacity
bullets: In a standard transformer, FLOPs per token are tied directly to total parameter count — want a smarter model, you pay for it on every token, including trivial ones
Pretraining compute and serving cost both scale with that same number, so growing capacity and keeping inference cheap pull in opposite directions
But not every token needs the full network: punctuation, common words, and easy continuations don't need the same depth of computation as a hard reasoning step

slides.title: Route Each Token to a Handful of Experts
bullets: Replace one big feed-forward network per layer with N smaller expert feed-forwards (commonly 8 to 256), each the same shape as a normal FFN
A tiny router — one linear layer plus a softmax over experts — scores every token, and only the top-k highest-scoring experts (commonly top-1 or top-2) actually run
The chosen experts' outputs are combined using the router's own scores as weights, so routing is differentiable and trained end-to-end rather than a hard switch

slides.title: Why Routing Needs a Balancing Act
bullets: Without correction, the router tends to collapse: a few experts get most of the traffic and keep improving, while the rest barely train — a rich-get-richer dynamic
The classic fix is an auxiliary load-balancing loss that penalizes uneven expert usage across a batch, nudging the router to spread tokens roughly evenly

DeepSeek-V3 instead uses an auxiliary-loss-free scheme: a per-expert bias term added only to the routing decision (not the training loss), adjusted up or down after each batch based on how overloaded or underused that expert was
Some designs also add always-on 'shared experts' that process every token alongside the routed ones, so common patterns don't need to be re-learned redundantly by every specialist

slides.title: Total Parameters vs. What Actually Runs
slides.body: Figures are from each model's public technical report; 'active params' is the portion actually computed per token, not counting always-on layers like attention.

rows: Learned subset of 256 routed experts + 1 shared expert

slides.title: Tracing a Single Token Through an MoE Layer
bullets: A token's hidden vector reaches an MoE layer with 8 experts; the router computes 8 scores and keeps only the top 2 — say expert #3 (weight 0.61) and expert #6 (weight 0.29), zeroing the rest
Only experts #3 and #6 run their feed-forward math on this token; the other 6 experts do zero work for it, even though their weights are sitting in accelerator memory the whole time

The two outputs are blended as a weighted sum using the renormalized router weights, and that becomes the layer's output for this one token — the very next token in the same sequence can route to a completely different pair of experts

Routing analyses of models like Mixtral have found experts often specialize by surface pattern — certain experts handling punctuation- or whitespace-heavy tokens — more than by clean topic boundaries; specialization is real but not always the intuitive kind

slides.title: The Catch: Sparse Compute, Dense Memory
bullets: Every expert's weights must sit in accelerator memory even though only a couple run per token — Mixtral needs roughly the memory footprint of a 47B dense model despite only ~13B active compute
Load balancing is a real tuning headache: too weak and routing collapses onto a few favorite experts; too strong and it hurts quality by forcing unnatural token-to-expert assignments
Distributed training and serving typically split experts across devices ('expert parallelism'), adding all-to-all communication overhead whenever tokens route to an expert living on another GPU

Skip MoE when: the dense equivalent already fits comfortably in memory, you're serving on a single GPU where the memory overhead can't be amortized across enough traffic, or your team lacks the infrastructure for expert-parallel training and serving

slides.title: The Core Idea to Remember
bullets: MoE decouples total parameter count from per-token compute: a model can hold huge capacity while only a small, learned slice fires for any given token
The router and its load-balancing mechanism — not the expert layers themselves — is where the real engineering difficulty lives
Memory, not compute, becomes the new bottleneck: every expert must stay resident even when idle

MoE is now the default architecture for the largest open-weight frontier models (Mixtral, DeepSeek-V3, and others), because it's the most practical way to keep adding capacity without a proportional rise in inference cost

questions.prompt: What does adding a Mixture-of-Experts layer actually change compared to a dense feed-forward layer?
options: It replaces one FFN with several smaller FFNs plus a router that activates only a few per token
It makes every parameter run on every token, just spread across more layers
It removes the feed-forward network entirely and relies only on attention
It compresses all the experts into a single shared matrix
questions.explanation: MoE's whole point is sparse activation: instead of one dense FFN doing all the work, N expert FFNs sit side by side and a learned router sends each token to only a few of them, so most of the model's parameters are idle for any given token.

questions.prompt: Mixtral 8x7B has about 47B total parameters. Roughly how many are actually used to process a single token?
options: All 47B, since routing only affects training
About 13B, since the router picks the top-2 of 8 experts per layer
About 7B, exactly one expert's worth
About 24B, roughly half the model
questions.explanation: Mixtral routes each token to 2 of its 8 experts per layer (top-2 routing), so only a fraction of the total 47B parameters actually computes on any given token — roughly 13B active — which is why it runs like a much smaller dense model despite its larger total size.

questions.prompt: What's the main memory-related tradeoff that comes with Mixture-of-Experts models?
options: They use less memory than a dense model of the same active-compute size, since unused experts are swapped to disk automatically
All experts' weights must stay resident in accelerator memory even though only a few run per token, so memory footprint tracks total parameters, not active compute
MoE models don't require a KV cache at all
Memory usage is identical across MoE models regardless of expert count
questions.explanation: Because any token could be routed to any expert, every expert's weights need to be loaded and ready — so despite sparse compute per token, MoE models have a memory footprint closer to their dense-equivalent size, which is why Mixtral needs roughly as much memory as a 47B dense model despite only ~13B active parameters doing work per token.

posts.title: Claude Haiku 5.5: A Small Model That Scores Like a Big One
posts.subtitle: Anthropic's cheapest, fastest small model yet closes most of the gap to frontier models
posts.summary: Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5 is built for high-volume, cost-sensitive work — summaries, classification, subagent calls — and it closes most of the quality gap to much pricier models while costing roughly 75% less on average to run than its predecessor. It's also the first Haiku-class model with an adjustable effort setting and computer-use support.

slides.title: Anthropic's Smallest Model Just Stopped Being the Compromise Pick
slides.body: Released October 7, 2026, Claude Haiku 5.5 is what Anthropic calls "the cheapest, fastest, and most capable small model we've ever released" — and the benchmark gap to its bigger siblings has shrunk a lot.

slides.title: High-Volume AI Work Doesn't Need a Frontier Model — It Needs a Cheap, Fast One
bullets: Summarizing threads, classifying tickets, compacting context, running subagent calls — these happen thousands of times a day, not once.
Running all of that through a flagship model like Opus or Sonnet 5.5 is wasteful: you're paying frontier prices for tasks that don't need frontier reasoning.
But historically, cheap small models meant a steep quality cliff — fast and cheap, or capable, rarely both.
Anthropic's bet with Haiku 5.5: narrow that cliff enough that small models become the default, not the fallback.

slides.title: What's Actually New: Effort Control, Subagent Fit, Computer Use
bullets: First Haiku-class model with an adjustable effort setting (Low, Med, High, Xhigh, Max) — trade latency for reasoning depth per request instead of switching models.
Designed to run as a subagent alongside Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 on coding work — the bigger model delegates routine subtasks down to Haiku.
Adds computer-use and browser-use support (beta in the Python and TypeScript SDKs) — a capability previously reserved for larger models.
Uses an updated tokenizer, which means it burns slightly more tokens per task than Haiku 4.5 did — a real tradeoff tucked inside the upgrade.

slides.title: The Benchmark Gap to Frontier Models Shrank Hard
slides.body: Anthropic's own published numbers show Haiku 5.5 roughly doubling Haiku 4.5's scores and closing a lot of distance to Sonnet 5.5 — at a fraction of the price.

slides.title: Early Customers Are Already Swapping It In
bullets: Asana reports over 30% lower latency on task completions and up to 2.5x faster inference per agent turn after switching to Haiku 5.5.
HubSpot hit 92.8% average across three runs of its CRM benchmark suite — the best score it had seen on that suite from any model.
AlphaSense scored 0.84 vs. 0.76 for Haiku 4.5 across 400 real queries — a meaningful jump for a model swap alone.
Cognition's Devin Fusion scored 66.2 on FrontierCode using Haiku 5.5 as its "sidekick" model for routine subtasks.

slides.title: The Catch: Tiered Pricing and Tighter Safety Rails
bullets: Pricing is tiered by prompt length: $0.10/$0.50 per million input/output tokens up to 100k tokens, rising to $0.50/$2.50 beyond that — the 'about 75% cheaper' headline is an average, not a flat rate.
Anthropic states the saving is closer to 90% for requests under 100k tokens but only about 50% above that threshold — read the footnotes before you budget off the headline number.
Cybersecurity safeguards are stricter than Haiku 4.5's (though looser than Sonnet 5.5's) and still block penetration-testing-style requests outright.
The updated tokenizer means token-based cost comparisons against Haiku 4.5 aren't quite apples-to-apples — the same prompt now costs slightly more tokens before the per-token price even applies.

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Claude Haiku 5.5 (Oct 7, 2026) roughly doubles Haiku 4.5's scores on tasks like OSWorld and Terminal-Bench while costing ~75% less on average to run.
It's the first Haiku-class model with an adjustable effort setting and the first to support computer use/browser use.
Real deployments (Asana, HubSpot, AlphaSense, Cognition) are already using it as a cheap subagent under bigger orchestrator models, not a standalone replacement.
Check the fine print on pricing tiers and the new tokenizer before assuming the 75% savings figure applies to your exact workload.

posts.title: Byte-Pair Encoding: How LLMs Turn Text Into Tokens
posts.subtitle: The unglamorous merge-table trick that decides what you're actually paying for
posts.summary: Before any LLM math happens, raw text is cut into tokens using a vocabulary built by Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) — repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols until a target vocabulary size is reached. That vocabulary is why context windows, API pricing, and even some bizarre model failures are measured in tokens, not words.

slides.title: Every LLM Call Starts By Cutting Your Text Into Pieces
slides.body: Models don't read words or letters directly — they read a sequence of tokens from a fixed vocabulary, and the way that vocabulary was built explains a surprising number of LLM quirks.

slides.title: Characters Are Too Fine-Grained, Whole Words Are Too Coarse
bullets: Character-level tokenization: tiny vocabulary (~256 bytes), but sequences get long — the model has to compose meaning across many more steps for the same sentence.
Word-level tokenization: short sequences, but the vocabulary explodes (English alone has well over 100,000 words) and any typo, name, or new word becomes an unknown token.
The out-of-vocabulary (OOV) problem is the real killer: a word-level model that's never seen 'tokenization' at training time has no way to represent it at all.
You need something in between — exact enough to represent anything, compact enough to keep sequences short.

slides.title: BPE: Keep Merging the Most Frequent Pair Until You Hit a Target Size
bullets: Start with every individual byte as its own token — a 256-symbol base vocabulary that can represent absolutely any text, including emoji and other languages.
Scan the training corpus, find the single most frequent adjacent pair of symbols, and merge it into one new token. Repeat, building a merge table thousands of entries deep.
Common fragments ('the', 'ing', 'tion') get merged into single tokens early because they're frequent; rare words stay split into several subword pieces.
GPT-2/GPT-3 used a ~50,257-token vocabulary; GPT-4's cl100k_base vocabulary has roughly 100,000 tokens — same merge-based idea, just more merges and more training data.

slides.title: Three Granularities, Three Different Tradeoffs
Why Your Bill and Your Context Window Are in Tokens, Not Words
bullets: OpenAI's own rule of thumb: one token is roughly 4 characters of English text, or about three-quarters of a word — so 'word count' and 'token count' are only loosely related.
A model with an English-heavy training corpus merges common English fragments into single tokens quickly, but text in other languages often matches fewer long merged tokens.
Practical effect: the same sentence translated into, say, Hindi or Japanese can cost noticeably more tokens on an English-centric tokenizer, because it fragments into more, shorter pieces.
This is why two prompts that feel equally long to a human reader can cost very different amounts against a per-token API price.

slides.title: Where Tokenization Quietly Causes Problems
bullets: Tokenizers are frozen at training time — you can't reuse one model family's token ids with another; switching model families means re-tokenizing raw text from scratch.

Rare or garbage substrings that showed up oddly in training data can earn their own token without the model ever learning a solid meaning for it, producing bizarre or unstable completions when that token appears — the well-documented 'glitch token' phenomenon.

Multi-digit numbers and individual letters inside a word often get glued into single tokens the model never explicitly learned to decompose, which is part of why LLMs can be surprisingly bad at digit-by-digit arithmetic or letter-counting inside long words.
None of this is a bug you can fix with a better prompt — it's a property of the fixed vocabulary baked in long before your prompt ever runs.

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: BPE builds a vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent symbol pair in the training corpus until it hits a target size — it's the bridge between character-level (no unknowns, long sequences) and word-level (short sequences, OOV failures).
Modern LLM vocabularies run from roughly 50,000 to 200,000 tokens, built the same merge-based way with more data and more merges.
Token count, not word or character count, governs context window usage and API billing — and it varies a lot by language and content type.
Tokenizer quirks (frozen vocabularies, glitch tokens, glued-together digits) explain real, otherwise-mysterious LLM failure modes.

questions.prompt: What problem does Byte-Pair Encoding solve that pure word-level tokenization can't?
options: Handling words never seen during training, by falling back to smaller known subword pieces
Making models understand grammar rules explicitly
Eliminating the need for a vocabulary entirely
Guaranteeing that one token always equals exactly one word
questions.explanation: Word-level vocabularies hit the out-of-vocabulary problem head-on — anything unseen becomes an unknown token. BPE's merge table can always fall back to smaller known pieces, down to individual bytes, so there's no truly unrepresentable input.

questions.prompt: Why can the same sentence cost more tokens in a non-English language than in English, on an English-trained BPE tokenizer?
options: Those languages inherently require more grammatical markers
The merge table was built mostly from an English-heavy corpus, so non-English text matches fewer long merged tokens and fragments into more, shorter pieces
Non-English scripts always use twice as many bytes per character
Tokenizers assign exactly one token per character in any language
questions.explanation: BPE's merges are frequency-driven from the training corpus. If that corpus skews English, English text matches long, frequent merged tokens while other languages fragment into many short tokens — raising token count and cost for equivalent content.

questions.prompt: A model from one family (50,000-token vocabulary) is swapped for a model from a different family (100,000-token vocabulary). What has to happen to reuse earlier conversation text?
options: Nothing — token ids are universal across all tokenizers
The text must be re-tokenized using the new model's own vocabulary and merge table, since token ids are specific to the tokenizer that produced them
Only the embedding layer needs updating, not the text itself
The context window automatically doubles to match
questions.explanation: Each tokenizer's merge table and id-to-token mapping is specific to how it was trained. The same numeric id means something different across two different vocabularies, so switching model families requires re-tokenizing the raw text, not reusing old token ids.

posts.title: Grouped-Query Attention: Fewer KV Heads, Faster Inference
posts.subtitle: The trick that let Llama 2 70B serve long contexts without drowning in cache
posts.summary: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) shrinks the KV cache by having several query heads share one key/value head instead of every head keeping its own. It interpolates between full Multi-Head Attention and single-head Multi-Query Attention, cutting memory and bandwidth with little quality loss — which is why Llama 2's larger models and Mistral 7B both use it.

slides.title: Serving LLMs Hits a Memory Wall Before a Compute Wall
slides.body: During generation, the bottleneck usually isn't FLOPs — it's how much key/value data you must keep resident in GPU memory for every token you've ever produced.

slides.title: The KV Cache Scales With Heads, Layers, and Tokens — All at Once
bullets: Autoregressive decoding reuses past keys/values instead of recomputing them — that's the KV cache.
In standard Multi-Head Attention (MHA), every attention head stores its own K and V vectors, per layer, per token.
Cache size = 2 (K+V) × layers × heads × head_dim × sequence_length × batch_size × bytes_per_value.
Double the context, double the cache. Double the batch, double it again — heads and layers are fixed multipliers on top.

slides.title: GQA: Split Query Heads Into Groups That Share One KV Head
bullets: Multi-Query Attention (MQA) is the extreme fix: every query head shares a single K/V head — huge memory savings, but quality drops.
Grouped-Query Attention (GQA, Ainslie et al. 2023) interpolates: query heads are split into g groups, and each group shares one KV head.
Llama 2 34B/70B use 64 query heads with only 8 KV heads — an 8:1 ratio. Mistral 7B uses 32 query heads with 8 KV heads.
Models aren't trained from scratch with GQA — they're 'uptrained' from an existing MHA checkpoint using roughly 5% of the original pretraining compute.

slides.title: MHA vs. GQA vs. MQA on a 64-Head Model
slides.body: The KV cache shrinks in exact proportion to how many KV heads you keep — quality degrades the same direction.

slides.title: One 4K-Token Sequence on Llama 2 70B: 10.7GB vs. 1.3GB
bullets: Llama 2 70B: 80 layers, head_dim 128, fp16 weights. A single 4096-token sequence, batch size 1.
With plain MHA (64 KV heads): 2 × 80 × 64 × 128 × 4096 × 2 bytes ≈ 10.7GB of KV cache for ONE sequence.
With GQA (8 KV heads, same model): the same formula with 8 instead of 64 ≈ 1.3GB — an 8x drop, straight from the head-count ratio.
That 8x is the difference between serving a handful of concurrent long-context requests per GPU and serving dozens.

slides.title: What GQA Doesn't Fix — and Where It Can Bite
bullets: GQA cuts memory and memory-bandwidth, not attention FLOPs — the query-side compute is unchanged, so it mainly helps memory-bound decoding, not prefill.
The group ratio is a tuned hyperparameter baked in at (up)training time — you can't change it after the fact to trade quality for memory at serving time.
Push the ratio too far toward MQA and retrieval-heavy or needle-in-haystack-style tasks degrade first, since fewer KV heads means less diversity in what gets attended to.
It's complementary to, not a substitute for, serving-side tricks like PagedAttention and continuous batching — those manage the smaller cache GQA already produced.

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: KV cache size, not raw compute, is often what limits how many requests an LLM server can hold concurrently.
GQA groups query heads to share KV heads, sliding between full MHA (best quality) and MQA (smallest cache).
Real ratios: Llama 2 70B uses 8:1, Mistral 7B uses 4:1 — not 1:1 and not all-the-way to MQA's 64:1.
Existing MHA checkpoints can be converted via lightweight uptraining rather than a full retrain from scratch.

questions.prompt: What does Grouped-Query Attention actually share across heads?
options: Key and value vectors across a group of query heads
The query vectors themselves across layers
The feed-forward weights across attention blocks
The positional embeddings across tokens
questions.explanation: GQA keeps every query head distinct but has a group of them read from one shared K/V head, which is exactly what shrinks the cache — the queries aren't shared, the keys/values are.

questions.prompt: Why does Llama 2 70B's KV cache shrink 8x when moving from MHA to its GQA setup?
options: It uses 8 KV heads instead of 64, and cache size scales linearly with KV head count
It reduces the sequence length by 8x during inference
It quantizes the KV cache from fp16 to fp16/8
It drops 8 of its 80 transformer layers at serving time
questions.explanation: Cache size is directly proportional to the number of KV heads. Going from 64 KV heads (MHA) to 8 (GQA) is an 8x reduction — nothing else in the formula changed.

questions.prompt: What's a real limitation of pushing GQA's ratio aggressively toward MQA (very few KV heads)?
options: Attention FLOPs for the query side increase sharply
Quality degrades first on retrieval-heavy or long-context tasks
The model can no longer be served with continuous batching
The sequence length limit is cut in half automatically
questions.explanation: Fewer KV heads means less diversity in what gets attended to, which shows up first on tasks that depend on precisely retrieving specific context — the memory savings come with a real quality cost at the extreme.

posts.title: MCP's Three Primitives: Tools, Resources, Prompts
posts.subtitle: One protocol, three building blocks — confuse them and your server is invisible to half the client
posts.summary: MCP servers don't expose one kind of thing — they expose three, each invoked differently: Tools the model calls to act, Resources the client reads for context, and Prompts the user picks to kick off a workflow. Mixing them up is why some MCP integrations feel broken.

slides.title: An MCP server isn't just 'a list of functions'
slides.body: It's tempting to treat Model Context Protocol as 'how I give the model more functions to call.' That's only a third of it. The spec defines three separate primitives, each with a different invoker and a different purpose.
bullets: Tools — invoked by the model, can have side effects
Resources — invoked by the client/user, read-only
Prompts — invoked by the user, pre-written workflow templates

slides.title: Treating everything as a Tool breaks the UX
slides.body: Server authors who only implement Tools end up forcing the model to 'call a function' just to fetch a file, a ticket, or a log — something a human should be able to pick directly from a file browser, with zero model calls.
bullets: A Tool call burns a model turn and tokens even for a plain read
Clients that render file pickers or @-mentions look for Resources — a Tools-only server has nothing to show there
The model decides when to call a Tool, so you lose deterministic, user-initiated access to your own data

slides.title: Tools: side-effecting actions the model chooses to invoke
slides.body: A Tool is the closest thing to a REST POST. The model sees a name, description, and JSON-Schema input, and decides at runtime whether and how to call it based on the conversation.
bullets: Declared with inputSchema; the client sends arguments the model generated
Expected to potentially mutate state — create_issue, send_email, run_query
Clients typically require explicit user approval before executing one, since the model is the one deciding to call it

slides.title: Resources: addressable, read-only context
slides.body: A Resource is closer to a REST GET: a URI-identified piece of content (a file, a DB row, a URL) that the client fetches and attaches to context — often without the model being involved in the decision at all.
bullets: Identified by a URI, e.g. repo://owner/name/path.py or postgres://db/table/42
Listable (resources/list) and fetchable (resources/read) — and subscribable, so a client can get notified when one changes
The user or client app decides to attach it; no model turn is spent deciding

slides.title: Prompts: user-triggered workflow templates
slides.body: A Prompt is a named, parameterized template the server exposes — the equivalent of a slash command. The user picks it; it expands into a ready-made message (often one that already references specific Resources).
bullets: Listed via prompts/list, each with a name and optional arguments
Invoking one returns a fully-formed set of messages the client inserts into the conversation
Used to package expert workflows — e.g. a /review-pr prompt that pre-attaches the right diff Resource and asks a specific question

slides.title: Same server, three different invokers
slides.body: The three primitives aren't interchangeable — they differ in who decides to use them and what they're allowed to do.
bullets: A single GitHub MCP server can expose all three without any overlap in purpose

slides.title: Worked example: reviewing a pull request
slides.body: A developer wants a PR reviewed using a GitHub MCP server that implements all three primitives correctly.
bullets: They type /review-pr 482 — a Prompt — which expands into a message that already embeds the diff
The diff itself was pulled in as a Resource (github://acme/api/pulls/482/diff), fetched by the client with no model call
Only after reading it does the model decide to call the post_review_comment Tool — a real side effect, gated by user approval
No step forced a Tool call just to read data, and no step needed the model to guess a URI from scratch

slides.title: Pitfalls worth knowing before you build
slides.body: Primitive choice isn't just style — picking the wrong one has real costs.
bullets: Making something a Tool when it's really a read wastes a model turn and loses cacheability — Resources can be fetched once and reused
Making something a Resource when it needs arguments or side effects doesn't fit — Resources don't take a model-decided input schema the way Tools do
Skipping Prompts means every workflow has to be re-explained in free text each time, instead of being a one-click, pre-tested template
A client that only implements the Tools half of the spec will silently never show your Resources or Prompts at all — check client capability support, not just server capability

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: MCP defines three primitives, not one: Tools (model-invoked, side-effecting), Resources (client-invoked, read-only, addressable by URI), Prompts (user-invoked templates)
Match the primitive to who should decide: the model for actions, the user/client for data access, the user for workflows
Resources are cacheable and subscribable; Tools cost a model turn and need approval; Prompts save everyone from retyping the same instructions
A Tools-only server works, but it's leaving two-thirds of the protocol — and a better UX — on the table

questions.prompt: Which MCP primitive is invoked by the model itself, mid-conversation, and expected to potentially cause side effects?
options: Resource
Prompt
Tool
Capability
questions.explanation: Tools are the model-invoked primitive — the model decides when to call one based on the conversation, and Tools are expected to be able to mutate state (create a ticket, send an email, run a query).

questions.prompt: A server wants to let a client's file picker show a repo's README without spending a model turn. Which primitive fits?
options: A Tool with no arguments
A Resource identified by a URI
A Prompt template
A capability negotiation flag
questions.explanation: Resources are read-only, URI-addressable content that the client or user can fetch directly — no model decision required, which is exactly what a file picker needs.

questions.prompt: Why might a client never show a server's Resources even though the server correctly implements them?
options: Resources are deprecated in MCP
The client only implements the Tools half of the spec, so Resource-specific UI (pickers, subscriptions) never renders
Resources require a paid subscription
Resources can only be used over stdio transport
questions.explanation: Client capability support varies — a client that never built Resource UI (file pickers, @-mentions, subscriptions) won't surface a server's Resources no matter how correctly the server implements them.

posts.title: Chunk Size Is a RAG Hyperparameter, Not a Detail
posts.subtitle: Split too small and you lose context; too big and retrieval drowns the right sentence in noise
posts.summary: How you split documents before embedding them decides what RAG can ever retrieve. Fixed-size chunking is the default and the most common source of silent retrieval failures — structure-aware and semantic chunking exist specifically to fix the failure modes fixed-size can't.

slides.title: Retrieval can't fix a bad chunk boundary
slides.body: No reranker or query rewrite can recover information that got split across two chunks and embedded separately. Chunking happens once, at ingest time — and it silently caps the ceiling on every query that comes after.
bullets: The most common RAG default: fixed-size, e.g. 512 tokens per chunk
The most common RAG failure: a chunk boundary lands mid-sentence, mid-table, or between a rule and its exception

slides.title: What fixed-size chunking actually breaks
slides.body: A 400-token sliding window doesn't know what a sentence, a clause, or a table row is — it just counts tokens and cuts.
bullets: A policy's eligibility rule ends up in chunk N, its exception clause in chunk N+1 — retrieve one and you get a confidently wrong answer
A markdown table's header row lands in one chunk, its data rows in another — the embedding for the data rows has no idea what the columns mean
Code gets cut mid-function, so the embedded chunk contains half a function signature and none of its body

slides.title: Four real strategies, in order of sophistication
slides.body: Each strategy trades implementation cost for how well it respects the document's actual structure.
bullets: Fixed-size + overlap — cheapest; cut every N tokens, overlap ~10-20% so a boundary-split idea appears whole in at least one chunk
Recursive structure-aware — split on headers/paragraphs first, only fall back to size-based cuts within a section that's still too big
Semantic chunking — embed consecutive sentences, cut where cosine similarity between neighbors drops sharply (a real topic shift)
Format-aware — markdown/code-specific splitters that never cut inside a table, code block, or list item

slides.title: Why overlap exists at all
slides.body: Overlap is a cheap insurance policy against the boundary problem, paid for in index size.
bullets: With 0% overlap, a sentence split across chunks 4 and 5 appears whole in neither — both embeddings are of a half-thought
With ~15% overlap (e.g. 75 tokens of a 512-token chunk repeated at the start of the next), that sentence appears complete in at least one of the two
Cost: a corpus chunked with 15% overlap needs roughly 15% more vectors stored and searched for the same source text

slides.title: Worked example: a 3-clause refund policy
slides.body: Source text: 'Refunds are issued within 14 days of purchase. Exception: digital goods are non-refundable once downloaded. Physical goods must be returned unopened.'
bullets: Fixed 20-token chunking with no overlap: chunk A ends at '...within 14 days of purchase,' chunk B starts at 'Exception: digital goods...' — a query about 'can I get a refund on an ebook' may retrieve only chunk A and answer yes, incorrectly
Structure-aware chunking that keeps each full sentence (or the whole clause-plus-exception) together retrieves the exception alongside the rule every time
The fix here wasn't a better reranker — it was never splitting the rule from its exception in the first place

slides.title: Picking a strategy by document type
slides.body: There's no single best chunker — the right default depends on what you're chunking.

rows: Dense technical prose with soft topic shifts

slides.title: When NOT to reach for semantic chunking
slides.body: Semantic chunking is the most 'sophisticated' option, which doesn't mean it's the best default.
bullets: It requires embedding every sentence before you even build chunks — doubles your embedding cost at ingest time
Similarity-drop cut points are non-deterministic across embedding model versions — re-indexing with a new model can shuffle your chunk boundaries entirely
For a markdown table or a code file, structure-aware splitting is strictly better and far cheaper — a table has a real, known boundary; don't let an embedding model guess at one
More overlap isn't free either: too much inflates the index and can return near-duplicate chunks that crowd out genuinely different results in top-k

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: Chunking is where most RAG retrieval failures are born — no amount of reranking recovers a fact split across two embeddings
Fixed-size + overlap is the cheap default; overlap (~10-20%) exists specifically to keep boundary-split ideas whole in at least one chunk
Structure-aware and format-aware chunking beat fixed-size whenever the source has real structure (headers, tables, code) — use the document's own boundaries first
Reach for semantic chunking only for dense, unstructured prose where topic shifts aren't marked by any heading — it's the most expensive option, not the default

questions.prompt: Why does chunk overlap help with the 'split sentence' problem?
options: It makes embeddings smaller
It repeats a slice of the previous chunk at the start of the next, so a boundary-split idea appears whole in at least one chunk
It removes the need for embeddings entirely
It guarantees chunks are semantically identical
questions.explanation: Overlap is insurance: by repeating the tail of one chunk at the head of the next, an idea that happened to fall on a boundary still appears intact in at least one chunk.

questions.prompt: A corpus is mostly markdown tables and code blocks. Which chunking strategy is the best default?
options: Semantic chunking by similarity drop
Fixed-size with no overlap
Format-aware chunking that never cuts inside a table or code block
Chunking by exact character count only
questions.explanation: Tables and code have real, known structural boundaries. A format-aware splitter respects them directly and cheaply — semantic chunking would waste compute guessing at a boundary that's already explicit in the syntax.

questions.prompt: What's a real downside of semantic (similarity-drop) chunking?
options: It can only be used on images
It requires embedding every sentence up front, and its cut points can shift if you later change embedding models
It never works on English text
It's identical in cost to fixed-size chunking
questions.explanation: Semantic chunking needs sentence-level embeddings before chunk boundaries even exist, and because those boundaries come from a model's similarity scores, they aren't stable across embedding model versions.

posts.title: Idempotency Keys: Making It Safe to Retry Anything
posts.subtitle: A client can resend the same request forever — the server just has to recognize it already happened
posts.summary: When a network call times out, the client can never tell whether the server finished the work or not — so it retries. Idempotency keys let the server recognize a retried request and return the original result instead of doing the work twice, turning 'maybe it happened twice' into a solved problem.

slides.title: The timeout that charges a card twice
slides.body: A client sends a $50 charge request. The server processes it, then the response is lost to a network blip before the client sees the 200. The client, seeing only a timeout, retries the exact same charge. Without protection, that's two charges for one purchase.
bullets: At-least-once delivery is the honest default for any network call — 'exactly once' isn't something the network gives you for free
The client cannot distinguish 'never processed' from 'processed but the response was lost'

slides.title: Why 'just don't retry' isn't the answer
slides.body: Not retrying is worse: it means every transient network blip becomes a permanent failure the user has to notice and fix by hand.
bullets: Retries are necessary for reliability — they're also exactly what causes duplicate side effects
The failure is invisible until it isn't: it shows up as a support ticket about a double charge, not a stack trace
This isn't fixable on the client side alone — only the server knows whether the original request actually completed

slides.title: The mechanism: a key the server remembers
slides.body: The client generates a unique key (typically a UUID) per logical operation — not per HTTP attempt — and sends it in a header, e.g. Idempotency-Key: 7b2e...  Every retry of that same logical operation reuses the identical key.
bullets: First time the server sees a key: it does the real work, then stores the key alongside the result
Every later request with that same key: the server skips the work and returns the stored result, unchanged
The key must be generated once per operation and reused across all retries of it — a fresh key per attempt defeats the whole mechanism

slides.title: What the server actually stores
slides.body: A minimal idempotency table needs the key as primary key, plus enough to detect misuse and return the right thing.
bullets: idempotency_key (primary key) — the client-supplied UUID
request_hash — a hash of the request body, to detect the same key being reused for a different payload
status — processing or completed, so a request arriving while the first is still in flight gets a 409 instead of running twice concurrently
response_body + expires_at — the stored result to replay, with a TTL (commonly 24h) so the table doesn't grow forever

slides.title: Worked example: the charge API, step by step
slides.body: Client calls POST /charges with Idempotency-Key: abc123. The request reaches the server, the charge succeeds at the payment processor, but the response is lost on the way back. The client's HTTP client times out at 30s and retries with the same key.
bullets: Server receives the retry, looks up abc123 in the idempotency table, finds status=completed
It returns the exact stored charge object from the first attempt — same charge ID, same amount — instead of calling the payment processor again
The customer is charged once; the client sees a successful response either way, on attempt 1 or attempt 2
If the retry arrives while attempt 1 is still mid-flight (status=processing), the server returns 409 Conflict rather than racing a second execution

slides.title: What each approach actually protects against

rows: No — two retries can both run before either finishes

slides.title: Where idempotency keys stop protecting you
slides.body: The mechanism is narrow by design — know its edges before you rely on it.
bullets: Key reused with a DIFFERENT request body is a client bug or an attack — compare the stored request_hash and reject the mismatch (422), don't silently replay the old result for new input
No expiry means the table grows forever; a TTL (and a cleanup job) is not optional at scale
It only guards one request — a multi-step workflow (charge, then ship, then email) that fails halfway needs a saga or outbox pattern on top, not just a key on step one
If the client generates a new key on every retry (a common mistake), the whole mechanism does nothing — the key must identify the operation, not the attempt

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: Networks give you at-least-once delivery by default — idempotency keys are how you get exactly-once-effect on top of that
The client generates one key per logical operation and reuses it on every retry; the server stores the key with the result and replays it on a repeat
A 'processing' status plus a transactional insert guards against concurrent retries racing each other, not just sequential ones
It protects one request, not a whole workflow — multi-step side effects still need sagas, outboxes, or compensating actions

questions.prompt: Why can't the client just decide not to retry a timed-out request instead?
options: Retries are always free and risk-free, so there's no tradeoff
Not retrying turns every transient network blip into a permanent user-visible failure, since the client can't know if the work actually completed
The server always replies within 1ms so timeouts can't happen
HTTP forbids retries by specification
questions.explanation: Retries exist because transient failures are common and recoverable — the real problem is that retries can also duplicate side effects, which is exactly what idempotency keys are for.

questions.prompt: A client retries a request with the same Idempotency-Key but a different request body than the original. What should the server do?
options: Silently process the new body and return its result
Silently return the old stored result as if nothing changed
Detect the mismatch via the stored request hash and reject it (e.g. 422) rather than reusing or reprocessing
Delete the idempotency key and start over
questions.explanation: A reused key with a different payload signals a bug or misuse. Comparing a stored request hash lets the server catch this instead of either silently replaying a stale result or processing unrelated input under the same key.

questions.prompt: An idempotency key alone fully protects a workflow that charges a card, then ships an order, then sends a confirmation email. True or false?
options: True — idempotency keys make the entire multi-step workflow safe to retry
False — the key only protects the single request it's attached to; a failure partway through the multi-step workflow needs a saga or outbox pattern on top
True, but only if the key is regenerated on every retry
False, because idempotency keys don't work with payments
questions.explanation: Idempotency keys dedupe one request. A workflow with several side-effecting steps that can fail partway through needs its own mechanism (sagas, outbox pattern, compensating actions) to stay consistent end to end.

posts.title: A2A: The Protocol for Agents Talking to Other Agents
posts.subtitle: MCP connects a model to its tools. A2A connects one agent to a completely different agent it doesn't trust or control.
posts.summary: Agent2Agent (A2A) is an open protocol, originally from Google and now governed under the Agentic AI Foundation alongside MCP, that lets independent AI agents — possibly built on different frameworks by different vendors — discover each other's capabilities and collaborate on a task without sharing internal memory, tools, or code.

slides.title: Your agent needs to call someone else's agent
slides.body: MCP standardized how one model talks to its own tools and data. A2A tackles a different problem: how does Agent A, built by your company, hand off work to Agent B, built by a totally different company, without either side peeking inside the other?
bullets: Originally published by Google, April 2025
Donated to the Linux Foundation, now developed under the Agentic AI Foundation (the same body Anthropic contributes Agent Skills to)
Treats every agent as a black box — only its advertised capabilities are visible

slides.title: Why MCP alone doesn't solve this
slides.body: MCP assumes one model orchestrating tools it can inspect and call directly. That breaks down once the 'tool' is itself a reasoning agent with its own state, running on infrastructure you don't control.
bullets: You can't just hand another company's agent your system prompt and memory — it may run on a different model, framework, or vendor entirely
Long-running work (hours or days) needs a way to check status, not just a single request/response call
Security: exposing an agent's internal tools to an outside caller is a much bigger blast radius than exposing a curated API

slides.title: The Agent Card: a resume an agent publishes about itself
slides.body: Every A2A-compatible agent publishes a JSON 'Agent Card' at a well-known URL on its domain, describing what it can do before anyone talks to it.
bullets: Lists the agent's skills, supported input/output types, and authentication requirements
Lets a calling agent decide which remote agent fits the task before sending any real work
Equivalent to a service's API docs, but written for another agent to parse automatically, not for a human

slides.title: A Task is a stateful conversation, not one call
slides.body: A2A wraps each unit of work in a Task object with an explicit lifecycle, so long jobs can be tracked, paused for clarification, and streamed instead of blocking on a single HTTP response.
bullets: States include submitted, working, input-required, completed, failed, and canceled
The remote agent can push the task to input-required mid-way to ask a clarifying question, then resume
Streaming updates travel over Server-Sent Events, so the caller sees progress on multi-hour jobs instead of a blank wait

slides.title: A2A and MCP solve different halves of the problem
slides.body: They're complementary, not competing — a single agentic system typically uses both at once.
bullets: A real stack: your agent uses MCP to call its own tools, then uses A2A to delegate a sub-task to a specialist agent from another team

rows: A model to tools and data sources
One agent to another independent agent
Agent Card published at a well-known URL
No — the remote agent stays a black box

slides.title: Worked example: a trip-planning agent
slides.body: Your travel-planning agent needs a flight booked. Instead of building flight-booking logic itself, it discovers an airline's A2A Agent Card, confirms it handles 'book-flight' tasks, and opens a Task with trip dates and passenger details.
bullets: The airline's agent may ask a clarifying question (input-required) if a fare class is ambiguous
Your agent never sees the airline's internal pricing engine, inventory system, or model — only the Task's messages and final Artifact (the itinerary)
If the airline later swaps its backend AI entirely, your integration doesn't need to change — the Agent Card contract stays the same

slides.title: Where it adds real cost and risk
slides.body: A2A is overhead you shouldn't pay when a simple function call or a shared MCP server would do.
bullets: Skip it for tools you own and fully trust — A2A's black-box isolation is wasted ceremony for an in-house function call
Opaque agents are also hard to debug: when a remote agent fails, you only see its Task status, not why
The protocol is young and still settling (transport bindings and even the Agent Card's file path have shifted between versions) — pin a spec version and expect churn
Letting an outside agent autonomously trigger paid actions (bookings, payments) needs its own authorization layer — A2A defines messaging, not business authorization

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: MCP wires a model to tools it controls; A2A wires one agent to an independent agent it doesn't control — different problems, same agentic stack
The Agent Card is the discovery mechanism: a machine-readable capability listing published at a well-known URL
Tasks carry an explicit lifecycle (submitted → working → input-required → completed/failed/canceled) so long, async agent work can be tracked and streamed
Don't reach for A2A to talk to tools you own — save it for crossing a real trust or vendor boundary

questions.prompt: What's the core difference between what MCP and A2A each standardize?
options: They're two competing standards for the exact same problem
MCP connects a model to tools/data it controls; A2A connects one agent to a separate, independent agent it doesn't control
MCP is for text models, A2A is for image models
A2A replaced MCP in 2026
questions.explanation: MCP standardizes model-to-tool access within your own system; A2A standardizes agent-to-agent collaboration across trust and vendor boundaries. They're meant to be used together.

questions.prompt: What does an A2A Agent Card do?
options: It stores the agent's private model weights
It's a JSON manifest, published at a well-known URL, listing an agent's skills and how to reach it — so other agents can discover it before sending work
It's a billing invoice sent after a task completes
It replaces the need for a Task object
questions.explanation: The Agent Card is a published capability listing — the equivalent of API docs written for another agent to parse automatically.

questions.prompt: Why does A2A model work as a stateful 'Task' with lifecycle states instead of one request/response call?
options: To make the protocol harder to implement
Because agent work can run long, may need mid-task clarification (input-required), and benefits from streamed progress updates rather than a single blocking response
Tasks are purely cosmetic and have no functional purpose
Because HTTP doesn't support JSON
questions.explanation: Real agent work can take hours, need a clarifying question mid-way, or require progress streaming — a single blocking call can't represent that, so A2A gives tasks an explicit lifecycle.

posts.title: What 66 Interviews Reveal About Real AI Adoption
posts.subtitle: Anthropic sat down with 58 companies mid-rollout. The honest picture is messier than the hype.
posts.summary: Anthropic's economics team interviewed 66 people across 58 companies mid-way through adopting AI and coded nearly 300 real use cases. The headline: most value comes from doing more, not firing people, and the companies that reorganize work around AI — instead of just automating or letting individuals freelance tools — get the most out of it.

slides.title: Inside 58 companies actually using AI
slides.body: Anthropic's Economic Index team ran 66 face-to-face interviews across 58 US companies — all Anthropic enterprise customers, all mid-rollout — then coded nearly 300 specific AI use cases for value and organizational impact.
bullets: Qualitative study, not a representative survey — self-reported value, not A/B-tested
Interviewees spanned executives, managers, and individual contributors
~300 'applications' (specific use case + specific company) were coded

slides.title: Most AI-transformation talk is still guesswork
slides.body: Executives and pundits argue about AI's effect on jobs and productivity largely from anecdotes or marketing claims. This report tried to ground that debate in what practitioners actually reported happening inside real companies.
bullets: No representative sample — results skew toward companies already committed to Anthropic's tools
Value assessments are mostly self-reported, not measured against a control group
The authors explicitly call for quantitative follow-up research

slides.title: The value is mostly output, not layoffs
slides.body: Across the ~300 coded use cases, roughly half of the reported output gains came from simply doing existing work faster, and half from better quality or entirely new products and services.
bullets: Only about 1 in 10 use cases delivered value directly to employees (lighter workload, more enjoyable work)
Of 100 software tools described in detail: 80% automated manual work, 20% replaced existing vendor software
Coding agents increasingly let non-technical staff build their own internal software

slides.title: What happened to headcount, in numbers
slides.body: Mass layoffs were rare. The bigger effect was on hiring plans and contractor spend, not existing full-time staff.
bullets: Six AI-native startups estimated they'd need roughly 4x their current headcount without AI
Customer skepticism and regulation were rarely cited as adoption barriers — most friction was internal

rows: Directly eliminated a position because of AI
Pushed out employees who refused to adopt AI
Hired more because of AI (mostly implementation/IT)

slides.title: Three ways companies actually adopt AI
slides.body: The report sorts adoption into three patterns, each with a different risk profile.
bullets: Top-down automation: vendors automate whole workflows — fast, but breeds job insecurity, expert resistance, and brittle systems that go stale as models improve
Bottom-up experimentation: individual employees build their own tools — real local wins, but gains don't spread and maintenance cost piles up on one person
Reorganization: companies broaden roles, redeploy staff to bottlenecks (review, judgment, product decisions), and build shared data/tooling infrastructure

slides.title: The 80-hour audit that became an afternoon
slides.body: A bottom-up example from the interviews: a non-technical employee built an internal tool that automated a 401(k) compliance audit previously taking about 80 hours of manual work per cycle.
bullets: Classic bottom-up win: built by the person who felt the pain, not by IT or a vendor
The catch the report flags: who maintains that tool when the model updates or the employee leaves?
Without reorganization around it, gains like this stay local instead of spreading company-wide

slides.title: The bottleneck isn't the model — it's review
slides.body: The report's biggest operational finding: once AI accelerates one part of a workflow, the parts that don't speed up (human review, sales, strategic decisions) become the new chokepoint.
bullets: Reviewing AI output at volume overwhelms human attention
Uneven adoption across employees creates internal friction and conflict
Many companies simply lack the data and infrastructure to let AI-built software run safely

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: Value from AI adoption came mostly from producing more, not cutting costs or headcount directly
Top-down automation and bottom-up tinkering both work short-term but carry real organizational risk
Reorganizing around AI — broadening roles, redeploying people to bottlenecks, sharing infrastructure — captured the most value in this sample
This is a qualitative snapshot of 58 companies already using Claude, not a universal law — treat the patterns as hypotheses, not guarantees

posts.title: MCP Elicitation: Letting Servers Ask Mid-Task
posts.subtitle: A protocol-level pause button so a tool call can ask the human something before it finishes.
posts.summary: MCP's elicitation feature lets a server pause a tool call and ask the connected human a question through the client, instead of guessing or failing outright. Form mode collects structured answers in-band; URL mode hands sensitive steps like payments or OAuth to an external page the client must show plainly before opening.

slides.title: When the Server Needs to Ask You Something
slides.body: Most MCP tool calls assume the model already has every answer. Elicitation gives a server a standard way to stop mid-task and ask the human directly, through the client.

slides.title: Before Elicitation, Servers Had Two Bad Options
slides.body: A tool call that needs missing information used to force a choice between guessing and refusing.
bullets: Guess the missing parameter and risk the model hallucinating a value it never actually had
Fail the call outright and push the burden back to the model to re-prompt the user in plain chat, with no structured way to collect the answer
Nothing let a server pause mid-execution, ask a scoped question, and resume with a validated answer

slides.title: elicitation/create: A Server-Initiated, Schema-Checked Question
slides.body: Clients declare an elicitation capability at initialization (form and/or url support); servers can then send an elicitation/create request mid-call.
bullets: Every request carries a 'mode' (form or url) and a human-readable 'message' explaining why the input is needed

Form mode adds a 'requestedSchema': a JSON Schema limited to a FLAT object of primitives — strings (with formats like email, uri, date, date-time), numbers, booleans, and enums — no nested objects or arrays
URL mode adds a 'url' and a unique 'elicitationId' instead of a schema; the client just opens the link, it doesn't see what happens there
The client's response is one of three actions: accept (with a schema-matching 'content' for form mode), decline, or cancel — servers must handle all three, not just accept

slides.title: Same Feature, Two Very Different Flows
slides.body: A travel-booking MCP server needs a seat preference; a checkout server needs a card number. Elicitation routes each through the mode built for it.
bullets: Form mode: server sends mode:'form' with a schema enum ['economy','business']; client renders a picker; user answers; response comes back as action:'accept', content:{cabin:'business'}
URL mode: server sends mode:'url' with a Stripe checkout link and an elicitationId; client must show the full URL and domain before opening it, since the LLM and client never see the card data
When the out-of-band step finishes, the server can push a notifications/elicitation/complete notification instead of making the client poll
If a tool is called before its required elicitation resolves, the spec defines a dedicated error: URLElicitationRequiredError, code -32042

slides.title: Form Mode vs. URL Mode

rows: Structured content IS exposed to the client/LLM
Only the URL is exposed; what happens at the link is opaque
Allowed for passwords / API keys / payment creds
No schema — just a url + elicitationId

slides.title: Where It Breaks: Phishing, Fatigue, and Identity
slides.body: Elicitation is a trust boundary, not just a UX nicety — the spec spends as much text on misuse as on mechanics.
bullets: URL mode is a built-in phishing vector: the spec requires clients to show the full URL and target domain and get explicit consent before opening it, and to never pre-fetch it
Servers must bind elicitation state to the authenticated user, not just a session ID, and verify the person completing a URL flow is the one who started it
Form mode's schema is deliberately restrictive — if you need nested data or file uploads, elicitation is the wrong tool; redesign the tool call instead
Every mid-task question is a round-trip the human must act on; overusing elicitation for parameters the model could reasonably infer just trains users to click 'accept' without reading

slides.title: A Standard Way to Say 'Wait, I Need to Ask You First'
bullets: Elicitation turns a silent guess-or-fail gap into a typed, capability-negotiated request/response pair
Use form mode for small, structured, non-sensitive answers; use url mode for anything that touches passwords, payment, or OAuth
accept / decline / cancel are all first-class outcomes — a server that only handles accept will break the first time a user hits Escape
The security burden sits mostly on the client (show the URL, bind to identity) and the server (never reuse MCP credentials for third-party services reached via URL mode)

questions.prompt: What does MCP's elicitation feature let a server do that a plain tool call can't?
options: Call another LLM to generate a sub-answer
Pause mid-task and ask the connected human a structured question through the client
Execute arbitrary shell commands on the client
Cache the result of a previous tool call
questions.explanation: Elicitation is specifically a server-to-human round trip mediated by the client — it's unrelated to sampling (server borrowing the client's model) or caching; it exists to fill in information the server doesn't have yet.

questions.prompt: Why can't a server use form mode to ask a user for their API key?
options: Form mode has no way to represent text input
Form-mode content is exposed to the client and LLM in-band, so the spec requires sensitive data like credentials to go through URL mode instead
Form mode is deprecated as of the latest spec
API keys must always be hardcoded in the server
questions.explanation: Form mode's answers are visible to the client (and potentially the LLM), so the spec explicitly prohibits using it for passwords, API keys, access tokens, or payment credentials — those must go through URL mode, which keeps the actual sensitive exchange out-of-band.

questions.prompt: What must a client do before opening a URL-mode elicitation link?
options: Silently pre-fetch it to check it's safe
Let the LLM decide whether to open it automatically
Show the user the full URL and target domain and get explicit consent first
Nothing — URL mode requires no client-side checks
questions.explanation: Because URL mode is a built-in phishing surface, the spec requires the client to display the full URL and domain and obtain explicit user consent before opening it, and never to pre-fetch it or let the model open it silently.

posts.title: GIC Forecasting: Predicting Grid Risk From Solar Storms
posts.subtitle: A physics-informed ML pipeline flags geomagnetic-storm risk for 66,935 US substations 30-60 minutes ahead.
posts.summary: Microsoft Research built a gradient-boosting pipeline that turns solar-wind readings into substation-level blackout risk scores 30-60 minutes before a geomagnetic storm hits, scoring all 66,935 continental-US substations in about a third of a second. It beats simple baselines on every forecast stage but still misses more than a third of the rarest, most extreme events.

slides.title: When the Sun Threatens the Grid
slides.body: A geomagnetic storm in 1989 blacked out Quebec in under two minutes. Microsoft Research built an ML pipeline to see storms like that coming, substation by substation.

slides.title: Geomagnetic Storms Punch Current Into the Grid Itself
slides.body: A fast-changing magnetic field induces 'geomagnetically induced currents' (GICs) directly in long transmission lines — current the grid was never designed to carry.
bullets: The key danger signal is dB/dt: how FAST the local magnetic field is changing, not just how strong the storm is
GICs can saturate transformer cores, causing overheating, tripped protection relays, and in the worst case permanent damage
Operators need lead time to act — shedding load or adjusting protection settings — but storms arrive with little warning

slides.title: Three Stages: Forecast the Storm, Model the Geology, Score the Grid
slides.body: The pipeline chains three ML stages so a single solar-wind reading becomes a risk score for every substation.
bullets: Stage 1: solar-wind measurements from the L1 Lagrange point (~1.5M km from Earth) feed forecasts of the AE and Dst storm indices
Stage 2: those forecasts combine with local geological conductivity and substation location features
Stage 3: a gradient-boosting model estimates dB/dt per substation, described as 'physics-informed' rather than purely statistical
Around 50 AI agents were used in development to explore candidate features, validation strategies, and model configurations

slides.title: Each Stage Beats Its Baseline — By Different Margins
slides.body: Detection gets harder exactly where it matters most: the rarest, most damaging events.

rows: 410.2 nT RMSE — beat empirical and solar-wind-only baselines
7.2 nT RMSE — beat the classic Burton equation on 62.2% of peak-activity hours

slides.title: A Storm Hits L1 — What Happens in the Next 30 Minutes
slides.body: Walk the pipeline end to end for one storm.
bullets: Solar wind at L1 shifts; the AE/Dst forecast stage projects a storm reaching Earth in 30-60 minutes
Per-substation geology and location features are combined with the forecast to estimate dB/dt everywhere at once
All 66,935 continental-US substations get a risk score in about 333 milliseconds
Risk concentrates at northern stations (closer to auroral-zone current systems), giving operators a ranked list instead of a single national alert

slides.title: The Rarer the Event, the Worse the Model Gets
slides.body: This is a forecasting tool, not a guarantee — and its own benchmark is thin.
bullets: Detection rate drops from 76.5% (major) to 64.1% (extreme) — the storms that do the most damage are the hardest to catch
False-alarm rate climbs as storm severity increases, trading missed events for more noisy warnings
The GIC-risk stage was only benchmarked against simple linear regression, because no widely deployed operational baseline exists to compare against
It's a decision-support signal for operators, not a substitute for hardened transformer protection

slides.title: Physics-Informed ML, Scored at Grid Scale
bullets: Chaining a space-weather forecast into a per-substation ML risk model turns a continental storm into actionable, location-specific warnings
~333ms to score 66,935 substations means this runs comfortably inside a 30-60 minute warning window
Every stage beats its baseline, but extreme-event detection (64.1%) is the real bottleneck, not raw speed
Real-world operational validation is still ahead — the current benchmark is against simple baselines, not deployed systems

questions.prompt: What is dB/dt, and why does the pipeline forecast it instead of just storm strength?
options: The storm's total energy output
The rate of change of the local magnetic field, which is what actually drives damaging induced currents
The distance between Earth and the L1 monitoring point
The number of substations affected
questions.explanation: Geomagnetically induced currents are driven by how fast the magnetic field changes (dB/dt), not just how strong a storm is overall — a slow-but-strong storm can be less dangerous than a fast-changing moderate one.

questions.prompt: Why does detection rate fall as event severity increases (76.5% major vs. 64.1% extreme)?
options: The model gets slower on bigger storms
Extreme events are rarer, so there's less training data and they're inherently harder to predict reliably
Extreme events don't produce measurable dB/dt
The L1 satellite can't observe extreme storms
questions.explanation: Extreme events are the rarest class, giving the model the least data to learn from — exactly the events where a miss matters most, which is the pipeline's clearest limitation.

questions.prompt: Why is the GIC-risk stage only compared against simple linear regression rather than an existing operational system?
options: Linear regression is the industry-standard benchmark
No widely deployed operational baseline for this task currently exists
The researchers chose not to run a fair comparison
Gradient boosting can only be compared to linear models
questions.explanation: The post states there's no widely deployed operational benchmark for substation-level GIC risk, so the comparison is against a simple baseline rather than a competing production system — a real gap in validating real-world impact.
