posts.title: PagedAttention: Virtual Memory for the KV Cache
posts.subtitle: vLLM's core trick borrows an OS idea to stop LLM serving from wasting most of its memory on padding.
posts.summary: PagedAttention is the memory-management technique behind vLLM: it splits each request's KV cache into fixed-size, non-contiguous blocks managed with a page table, the same idea operating systems use for virtual memory. That cuts KV cache waste from 60-80% down to under 4% and enables cheap sharing of common prefixes across requests.

slides.title: Memory, Not Compute, Is the LLM-Serving Bottleneck
slides.body: Every token a model generates needs its key/value vectors kept around for attention — and at scale, how you store those vectors matters as much as the model itself.
bullets: The KV cache grows with every generated token
Naive allocation wastes most of that memory
vLLM's fix borrows a 1960s operating-systems idea

slides.title: Why Naive KV Cache Allocation Wastes Memory
slides.body: Early serving systems reserved one contiguous memory block sized for the maximum possible sequence length, per request.
bullets: Internal fragmentation: most requests finish long before hitting the max length, so most of the reserved block sits empty
External fragmentation: variable request lengths leave oddly-sized unusable gaps between allocations
No sharing: two requests with an identical system prompt each get their own separate copy
Original measurements found 60-80% of reserved KV cache memory went unused

slides.title: Borrowing Virtual Memory from the OS
slides.body: Instead of one contiguous block per request, PagedAttention splits the KV cache into small fixed-size blocks ("pages") that don't need to sit next to each other in memory.
bullets: Each sequence gets a logical-to-physical block table, just like a process's page table
Blocks are allocated on demand as new tokens are generated — not reserved up front
The attention kernel reads through the block table instead of assuming one flat contiguous buffer

slides.title: Copy-on-Write Makes Sharing Almost Free
slides.body: Because blocks are indirect, multiple sequences can point at the same physical block until one of them needs to change it.
bullets: Parallel sampling / beam search: many candidate continuations share the same prefix blocks, diverging only at the branch point
Shared system prompts: hundreds of concurrent requests with an identical prompt share one set of physical blocks
Only the diverging block gets copied — not the whole sequence's cache

slides.title: What Changed in Practice
slides.body: Figures from the original vLLM paper, comparing against prior serving systems like FasterTransformer and Orca.

slides.title: 100 Chat Sessions, One Shared System Prompt
slides.body: Say 100 users are chatting with an assistant that has a 2,000-token system prompt.
bullets: Without paging: 100 copies of that prompt's KV cache, even though every byte is identical
With PagedAttention: one set of physical blocks for the shared prefix, referenced by all 100 sequences
Each session only needs new physical blocks for the tokens it generates on top of that shared prefix

slides.title: Where It Doesn't Help — or Adds Cost
slides.body: Block-table indirection isn't free, and the benefit depends on your workload.
bullets: Every attention step now does a lookup through the block table instead of a flat memory read — a small but real overhead
Block size is a tuning knob: too small and that per-block overhead dominates; too large and you're back to wasting memory
If you're serving one request at a time with no shared prefixes (e.g. a single local user), there's little fragmentation to save in the first place
The win scales with concurrency — it matters most when you're batching many simultaneous requests

slides.title: The Idea Generalizes Past LLMs
slides.body: Treat scarce memory as pageable and shareable, not pre-reserved and private.
bullets: PagedAttention is why vLLM can push far higher batch sizes on the same GPU memory than naive serving code
Copy-on-write block sharing is the same trick that made OS process forking cheap, repurposed for attention caches
It's foundational to nearly every production LLM-serving stack today — understanding it explains why serving frameworks look the way they do

questions.prompt: What operating-system concept does PagedAttention borrow?
options: Garbage collection
Virtual memory / paging with non-contiguous blocks and a page table
Process scheduling priorities
File system journaling
questions.explanation: PagedAttention splits the KV cache into fixed-size blocks mapped through a logical-to-physical table, mirroring how OS virtual memory avoids needing one giant contiguous allocation per process.

questions.prompt: Roughly how much KV cache memory did naive, contiguous pre-allocation waste before PagedAttention?
options: Under 5%
About 20%
Nearly 100%
questions.explanation: Reserving a worst-case contiguous block per request wasted 60-80% of KV cache memory in the original measurements — most of it reserved but never used.

questions.prompt: Which serving scenario benefits most from PagedAttention's copy-on-write block sharing?
options: A single user running one request at a time locally
Many concurrent requests sharing a prefix, like beam search or a common system prompt
Training a model from scratch
Compressing model weights to int4
questions.explanation: Copy-on-write lets many sequences point at the same physical blocks until they diverge — a big win exactly when many requests share a prefix, as in beam search or a shared system prompt across concurrent chats.

posts.title: Contextual Retrieval: Giving Chunks Back Their Context
posts.subtitle: Prepending a short, LLM-written note to each chunk cuts retrieval failures by two-thirds.
posts.summary: Standard RAG strips chunks of the surrounding context that makes them findable. Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval has an LLM write a short note situating each chunk before it's embedded and indexed — cutting top-20 retrieval failures from 5.7% to 1.9% when combined with reranking, for about $1.02 per million document tokens thanks to prompt caching.

slides.title: Contextual Retrieval: Giving Chunks Back Their Context
slides.body: Anthropic's technique prepends a short, LLM-written summary to each chunk before embedding and indexing it — cutting retrieval failures by up to 67% when combined with reranking.
bullets: Baseline top-20 retrieval failure rate: 5.7%. Contextual embeddings + contextual BM25 + reranking: 1.9% — a 67% reduction
The fix costs about $1.02 per million document tokens, one time, thanks to prompt caching

slides.title: A Chunk Out of Context Is Often Useless
slides.body: Splitting documents into chunks for embedding strips away the surrounding context that makes a chunk findable.
bullets: Example chunk: 'The company's revenue grew by 3% over the previous quarter.' — no company name, no quarter, no fiscal year
A query for 'ACME Corp Q2 2023 revenue growth' won't match this chunk on keywords, and its embedding alone may not rank it highly either
This is exactly the failure mode standard RAG pipelines hit on multi-document corpora — SEC filings, legal contracts, long manuals

slides.title: Prepend Context Before You Embed or Index
slides.body: For each chunk, Claude reads the whole document plus that chunk and writes a short note — typically 50 to 100 tokens — that situates the chunk within the document. That note gets prepended to the chunk before generating embeddings and building the BM25 keyword index.
bullets: Two indexes get the contextualized text: a vector embedding index AND a BM25 lexical index — contextual embeddings catch semantic matches, contextual BM25 catches exact terms like IDs or codenames embeddings miss

Prompt caching keeps this affordable: the full document loads into the cache once, so writing context for every chunk doesn't mean re-paying for the whole document each time — about $1.02 per million document tokens, one-time

slides.title: Each Layer Compounds — None Alone Gets You All the Way
slides.body: Anthropic measured top-20 retrieval failure rate (1 minus recall@20) across methods on the same eval set.
bullets: Reranking adds a second stage: retrieve the top 150 chunks, score them with a reranker, then keep only the top 20 that actually go to the model

slides.title: Worked Example: Finding One Fact in a Pile of SEC Filings
slides.body: Picture a RAG system over hundreds of 10-Q filings from different companies and quarters.
bullets: Raw chunk: 'The company's revenue grew by 3% over the previous quarter.' Contextualized chunk: 'This chunk is from ACME Corp's Q2 2023 10-Q, in the Results of Operations section. Original chunk: The company's revenue grew by 3% over the previous quarter.'
A query like 'Which companies grew revenue in Q2 2023?' can now match the contextualized chunk on both the embedding (semantic: revenue growth) and BM25 (exact terms: 'ACME Corp', 'Q2 2023')
Without that context, the same boilerplate chunk could just as easily surface for a dozen other companies' Q2 filings with near-identical phrasing

slides.title: When Contextual Retrieval Isn't Worth It
slides.body: The technique adds real engineering and reindexing cost, and it doesn't fix every retrieval problem.
bullets: If your corpus is small enough to fit in context directly, skip retrieval altogether — contextual retrieval is a tax on a problem you may not have
Chunks that are already self-contained (short FAQ entries, atomic facts) gain little — you pay LLM generation cost for near-zero benefit
Reranking adds latency (a second scoring pass over ~150 candidates) — fine for most chat use cases, often too slow for sub-100ms retrieval
Context generation is itself LLM output — a wrong or misleading summary introduces a new failure mode rather than removing one

slides.title: Context Is Retrieval Infrastructure, Not an Afterthought
bullets: Prepending a 50-100 token, LLM-written note to each chunk before embedding and BM25 indexing cut retrieval failures from 5.7% to 1.9% — a 67% reduction, stacked with reranking
Semantic (embeddings) and lexical (BM25) contextualization catch different failure modes — combine both rather than picking one
Prompt caching is what makes this economical: about $1.02 per million document tokens, paid once, not per chunk
Skip it for small corpora or already self-contained chunks — the cost only pays off when chunks genuinely lose meaning in isolation

questions.prompt: In Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval, what gets prepended to each chunk before indexing?
options: The full original document text
A short, LLM-written note (50-100 tokens) that situates the chunk within the document
A random unique identifier
The query the user is expected to ask
questions.explanation: The context is a short summary the LLM writes by reading the full document plus the chunk — not the whole document itself, which would make chunks huge and redundant.

questions.prompt: Why does Contextual Retrieval update BOTH the embedding index and the BM25 index with the contextualized chunk?
options: BM25 doesn't support indexing at all, so embeddings have to do double duty
Embeddings catch semantic similarity while BM25 catches exact keyword/term matches the embedding might miss — they fail differently
It's required by the vector database's API
BM25 is only used as a fallback when the embedding model is down
questions.explanation: Embeddings and BM25 have different blind spots; contextualizing both compounds the benefit — contextual embeddings alone cut failures 35%, adding contextual BM25 pushed it to 49%.

questions.prompt: What makes Contextual Retrieval economically practical at scale, according to Anthropic's reported cost?
options: The documents are compressed before processing
Prompt caching lets the full document load into cache once, so generating context for many chunks doesn't re-pay for the whole document each time
Only the first 10% of each document is ever read
Context is generated by a much smaller, free model
questions.explanation: Without caching, writing a context note per chunk would mean re-sending the entire source document for every chunk in that document. Caching brings the one-time cost to about $1.02 per million document tokens.

posts.title: AlphaGenome 2: DeepMind Reads DNA Cell by Cell
posts.subtitle: A sequence model that scores each DNA variant separately per cell type, not blended across a whole tissue.
posts.summary: Google DeepMind's AlphaGenome 2 predicts how a DNA variant changes gene expression separately for each cell type, instead of averaging across a whole tissue. On the TenK10K immune-cell benchmark it nearly doubled recall of likely causal variants at the same precision as its predecessor — but DeepMind is explicit it's a research prioritization tool, not a diagnostic one.

bullets: Trained on 100M+ single-cell profiles across 68 tissues
Built on Google DeepMind's earlier AlphaGenome regulatory-DNA model
Available now via the AlphaGenome API
slides.body: Announced November 11, 2026, AlphaGenome 2 predicts how a single DNA variant shifts gene activity — separately for each cell type, not as one blended tissue-wide score.
slides.title: A DNA Model That Thinks in Cell Types

bullets: Disease-relevant effects are often cell-type-specific (e.g. only in one immune cell subtype)
Bulk-tissue scoring averages over many cell types, burying rare but dangerous effects
The original AlphaGenome modeled regulatory DNA well, but single-cell resolution needed a different approach, not just fine-tuning
slides.body: Most variant-effect models score a mutation once per tissue, blending dozens of cell types into a single number. A variant that's disruptive in one rare cell type but neutral everywhere else gets diluted into "probably fine."
slides.title: Averaging Across a Tissue Hides the Signal

bullets: Trained on 100M+ individual cell profiles (bulk + single-cell, human + mouse) spanning 68 tissues
Output: a probability that a given variant shifts expression in that specific cell type or state
The gain comes from the narrower, cell-type-explicit target, not just more training data
slides.body: AlphaGenome 2 narrows its prediction target to a single cell type or state per pass, with an architecture built around that narrower focus rather than one global head covering every cell type at once.
slides.title: Predict One Cell Type at a Time, Explicitly

bullets: Benchmark: TenK10K — 28 distinct immune cell types
Even at 90% precision, AlphaGenome 2 still recovers only a minority of variants statistically nominated as causal — DeepMind states this limit explicitly
slides.body: On TenK10K, a benchmark spanning 28 immune cell types, AlphaGenome 2 recovers roughly twice as many of the putatively causal expression-linked variants as AlphaGenome 1, at the same 90% precision bar.
slides.title: Nearly Double the Causal Variants Found

bullets: Query: does variant X alter expression in T-cells vs. B-cells vs. monocytes? AlphaGenome 2 scores it per cell type
Lets a lab prioritize wet-lab validation to the one or two cell types where the effect is real, instead of testing all of them
Open now: AlphaGenome API for non-commercial research; private preview for commercial use
slides.body: A lab studying a variant linked to autoimmune disease wants to know which of roughly fifteen immune cell types it actually disrupts — not just "immune cells" in general.
slides.title: Why a Biologist Would Actually Use This

bullets: DeepMind states AlphaGenome 2 has not been validated or approved for clinical or diagnostic use
Trained predominantly on human and mouse reference data — rarer populations and variant types are less represented
A high-confidence score is a shortlist signal, not proof — wet-lab validation is still required
slides.body: The model is explicitly positioned as a research prioritization tool, with real limits DeepMind calls out itself.
slides.title: Not a Diagnostic Tool — DeepMind Says So Directly

bullets: Resolution mattered as much as scale here: narrowing the prediction target to one cell type nearly doubled recall at fixed precision
Bulk-tissue variant scoring quietly discards rare-cell-type effects — don't trust a tissue-average score for a disease you suspect is cell-type-specific
Even a state-of-the-art model here only catches a minority of true causal variants — treat its output as a prioritized shortlist, not a verdict
slides.title: Takeaways

questions.explanation: AlphaGenome 2's key change is resolution: instead of one blended score per tissue, it predicts expression effects separately per cell type, which is what let it catch effects bulk models average away.

options: The same tissue-wide average score, just computed faster
A separate prediction for each individual cell type or state
Whether the variant is inherited or arose de novo
The 3D protein structure the variant produces

questions.explanation: DeepMind reports AlphaGenome 2 recovering about 30% of putatively causal expression-linked variants at 90% precision, versus 16% for AlphaGenome 1 — nearly double.

options: Identical recall, just faster inference
Recovered about 30% of causal variants vs. about 16% for AlphaGenome 1
Recovered 100% of causal variants
Performed worse because of the narrower focus

options: It's too slow to run in a clinical setting

It only works on mouse DNA
It requires specialized hardware unavailable outside DeepMind

posts.title: Hybrid Search: Fusing Keyword and Vector Ranks
posts.subtitle: Why production RAG systems run BM25 and embeddings side by side, then merge the rankings by position, not score.
posts.summary: Vector search and keyword (BM25) search fail on opposite query types — embeddings blur exact rare terms, BM25 misses paraphrase and synonyms. Hybrid search runs both and fuses the ranked lists with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, which combines by rank position instead of raw score so incompatible scales never need normalizing.

bullets: Pure vector search misses exact matches: product codes, names, acronyms
Pure keyword search (BM25) misses paraphrases and synonyms
Hybrid search covers both failure modes at once
slides.body: Hybrid search runs a keyword retriever and a vector retriever on the same query, then fuses their rankings into one list.
slides.title: Two Search Engines, One Ranked List

bullets: A query like "error E-4502" can embed close to many unrelated error messages — the model doesn't know "4502" is the load-bearing token
BM25 (term frequency / inverse document frequency) nails exact and rare-term matches but can't see that "car" and "automobile" mean the same thing
Neither retriever dominates the other across query types — that's the actual case for hybrid, not redundancy
slides.body: Dense embeddings are trained to cluster semantically similar text, which makes them weak at treating one rare token — an error code, a SKU, a name — as the single most important signal in a query.
slides.title: Why Embeddings Alone Fail on Exact Terms

bullets: RRF score for a document = sum over each retriever of 1 / (k + rank in that list), with k = 60 as the canonical default (from Cormack et al., SIGIR 2009)
A document ranked #1 by vector search and #3 by BM25 beats one ranked #1 by only one retriever and absent from the other
No score normalization needed — this is RRF's main advantage over naive weighted-score blending
slides.body: RRF combines two ranked lists by rank position, not raw similarity score — which matters because BM25 scores and cosine similarities live on incompatible scales and can't be averaged directly.
slides.title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion Merges Rankings Without Scores

bullets: 1. The same query goes to both a keyword index (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Postgres tsvector) and a vector index (HNSW)
2. Each returns its own top-K ranked list, commonly K = 50-100
3. RRF merges the two ranked lists into one fused ranking
4. Optional: a cross-encoder reranker re-scores the fused top-N before it reaches the LLM
slides.title: What a Hybrid Pipeline Actually Looks Like

slides.body: Vector-database vendors (Weaviate, Qdrant, Pinecone) consistently report hybrid retrieval improving recall over either retriever alone on mixed query sets — the exact margin varies by corpus and query mix, so treat it as a qualitative, repeatedly-observed effect rather than one fixed number.

rows: Extra infra; fusion constant k needs tuning

slides.title: Hybrid Covers Both Retrievers' Blind Spots

bullets: BM25 nails "error -50" and "CarPlay" — exact strings a vector model might blur into a generic "connection error" chunk
Vector search nails documents describing the same bug in different words ("Bluetooth pairing fails silently") that never mention "-50" at all
RRF fusion surfaces both documents, instead of only the family of matches one retriever happens to favor
slides.body: Query: "Why does my phone throw error -50 when connecting to CarPlay?"
slides.title: A Concrete Query Where Hybrid Wins

bullets: Doubles retrieval infrastructure: a keyword index and a vector index now have to stay in sync
RRF's k constant and each retriever's top-K are tuning knobs — defaults aren't free for every corpus
For small corpora (a few thousand docs) or purely conversational queries, the extra BM25 leg often isn't worth the added latency
Doesn't fix bad chunking — low-quality chunks still rank highly in both retrievers
slides.title: When Hybrid Search Isn't Worth It

bullets: Vector and keyword search fail on opposite query types — hybrid isn't redundancy, it's covering each other's blind spot
RRF fuses by rank, not raw score, which is why it works without normalizing BM25 and cosine similarity onto the same scale
Add a reranker on top of the fused list for the last few points of precision — fusion buys recall, reranking buys precision
slides.title: Takeaways

questions.explanation: BM25 and cosine similarity have no shared scale — RRF sidesteps the problem by fusing rank positions (1/(k+rank)) instead of raw scores.
questions.prompt: Why can't you just average a BM25 score and a cosine similarity score directly?
options: They're both already normalized to 0-1, so it's fine to average them
They live on incompatible scales with different distributions, so RRF fuses by rank position instead
BM25 scores are always higher, so averaging is biased by design
Cosine similarity can be negative, which breaks addition

questions.explanation: BM25's IDF term gives rare tokens like exact error codes outsized weight, which is exactly what dense embeddings tend to blur across semantically similar text.
questions.prompt: A query contains a rare product error code like "E-4502". Which retriever is most likely to find the exact document mentioning it, and why?
options: Vector search, because embeddings generalize better
BM25/keyword search, because it weights rare exact terms heavily via inverse document frequency
Neither — exact codes can't be retrieved by either method
A cross-encoder reranker alone, with no first-stage retrieval needed

questions.explanation: Hybrid search adds real infrastructure and tuning cost (two indexes, fusion constant k, top-K per retriever) — worthwhile for mixed query workloads, but overkill for small or purely conversational corpora.
questions.prompt: What's a real downside of adding hybrid (BM25 + vector) search to a RAG pipeline?
options: It makes semantic queries impossible to answer
It requires maintaining two indexes in sync and tuning fusion parameters, which isn't worth it for every corpus
It only works with one specific embedding provider
BM25 can't be combined with an HNSW index at all

posts.title: Claude Fable 5.2: Built to Delegate, Not Just Answer
posts.subtitle: Anthropic's newest model is designed to advise and orchestrate smaller models, matching Opus 5.5 at a fraction of the cost.
posts.summary: Anthropic shipped Claude Fable 5.2 (and the restricted Mythos 5.2) on Nov 9, 2026 — a model built to act as an 'Advisor' or 'Orchestrator' that delegates work to smaller models, using tunable effort levels to match Opus 5.5 on many benchmarks at a fraction of the price. Real-world feats include a 1,000-agent Lean formalization of Fermat's Last Theorem in 30 hours and a production Python-to-Rust migration.

slides.title: A model whose real job is to delegate
slides.body: Claude Fable 5.2, announced November 9, 2026, isn't pitched as 'the new biggest model' — it's pitched as the one that decides what deserves its own reasoning and what a cheaper model can handle.
bullets: Shipped alongside the more-restricted Claude Mythos 5.2
API model ID: claude-fable-5-2
Available on direct API, AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure

slides.title: Frontier models are now too expensive to use on everything
slides.body: Agentic workflows can run for hours or days, generating thousands of sub-tasks. Routing every one of them through a flagship model burns money and time on work a smaller model could finish just as well.
bullets: Anthropic's own fix: give the flagship model two extra jobs — 'Advisor' (consulted by smaller models) and 'Orchestrator' (delegates simpler steps itself)
Anthropic still recommends Opus 5.5 as the daily driver, reserving Fable/Mythos for the hardest tasks
An effort knob (Low / Medium / High / Xhigh) lets the same model trade cost for accuracy per request

slides.title: Effort levels turn one model into a cost dial
slides.body: Instead of picking between separate cheap/expensive models, Fable 5.2 exposes an effort parameter, so the same weights can run cheap-and-fast or slow-and-thorough depending on the task.
bullets: FrontierCode 2.0 (agentic coding) at Xhigh effort: 49.1% — highest score of any released model tested
At High effort, FrontierCode 2.0 is ~45.3%, roughly tying Opus 5.5's best score at about half the cost per task
On Humanity's Last Exam (with tools), Low effort matches Opus 5.5's top score at under one-tenth the cost
Fast mode: up to 2.5x faster token generation for 2x the price ($16/$80 per million tokens vs. $8/$40 standard)

slides.title: Where it actually lands versus the competition
slides.body: Anthropic's own benchmark table (Fable 5.2 at its best effort setting) shows gains that are real but uneven — it doesn't win everything.
bullets: Note AutomationBench: Gemini 4 Carbon (53.9%) still beats Fable 5.2 (51.4%) on business-workflow automation

slides.title: 1,000 agents, 30 hours, one 90-year-old theorem
slides.body: Anthropic had a team of roughly 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents formalize Fermat's Last Theorem in the Lean proof assistant.
bullets: Completed in 30 hours with minimal human input, versus 11 days for the earlier formalization effort
Used about one-third as many action tokens and produced a proof seven times shorter
Opus 5.5, given the same task, reached only 26% completion after 18 hours
Separately: a team of agents migrated a production service from Python to Rust, and the rewritten service starts about 26x faster

slides.title: Where it's deliberately held back — and why that matters
slides.body: Some of Fable 5.2's limits are safety choices, not capability gaps, and the effort dial itself has a failure mode.
bullets: Anti-distillation defenses cut how much a competitor can learn by training on Fable's outputs by 90–99%, which also makes it a worse 'teacher' model for anyone
Training deliberately capped the model's own AI-R&D skills (e.g., accelerator kernel optimization) at roughly Opus 5.5's level, as a safety measure — it isn't trying to out-improve itself
Picking the wrong effort level wastes money (Xhigh on a trivial task) or underperforms (Low on a genuinely hard one) — it must be tuned per task, not set once
Mythos 5.2's expanded capabilities (cyber, biology) are gated behind Anthropic's Verification Programs, not available to general users

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: Fable 5.2's pitch isn't just 'smarter' — it's 'smarter about knowing when not to think as hard', via Advisor/Orchestrator roles and a tunable effort dial
On several agentic and coding benchmarks it matches or beats Opus 5.5 at a fraction of the cost when effort is tuned well
Real engineering results (Lean proof, Rust migration, generated circuit boards) back up the benchmark claims with concrete numbers
It's uneven, not universal — some benchmarks (like AutomationBench) still favor competitors, and some capabilities are intentionally capped or gated

questions.prompt: What's the main product idea behind Fable 5.2, beyond raw capability?
options: It's simply a bigger model than Opus 5.5
It's built to act as an Advisor or Orchestrator that delegates simpler work to smaller models
It only runs offline, with no API access
It replaces Claude Code entirely
questions.explanation: Anthropic designed Fable 5.2 to be consulted by smaller models ('Advisor') or to delegate sub-tasks itself ('Orchestrator'), rather than just being a bigger standalone model.

questions.prompt: What does the 'effort level' setting actually trade off?
options: Context window size for speed
Cost and speed for accuracy — e.g., Low effort can match Opus 5.5's best HLE score at under 1/10th the cost
Output language for latency
It has no measurable effect on benchmarks
questions.explanation: Effort level lets the same model run cheaper/faster or slower/more-thorough per request — on Humanity's Last Exam, Low effort reportedly matched Opus 5.5's top score at under a tenth of the cost.

questions.prompt: Why did ~1,000 Fable 5.2 agents formalize Fermat's Last Theorem in 30 hours when the earlier effort took 11 days?
options: The theorem was simplified for this attempt
Massive agent parallelism plus more efficient reasoning (about 1/3 the action tokens) let many agents work on sub-proofs concurrently
Anthropic used a specialized math-only model instead
It didn't — both efforts took the same time
questions.explanation: The gain came from running huge numbers of agents in parallel on sub-proofs, combined with more token-efficient reasoning per agent — not from a shortcut on the theorem itself.

posts.title: Prompt Caching: Paying Once to Reread the Same Context
posts.subtitle: Why reusing a model's own attention state — not just the text — is what makes long system prompts affordable.
posts.summary: Prompt caching lets an LLM provider store the computed attention state (KV cache) for a prompt prefix and reuse it on later requests, instead of reprocessing the same system prompt, tool definitions, or documents from scratch every call. Done right, it cuts both cost and time-to-first-token dramatically for agents and long multi-turn conversations — but it's brittle to prompt ordering and short-lived by default.

slides.title: You're paying full price to reread the same page
slides.body: Every API call to an LLM reprocesses its entire input from scratch by default — even if 95% of that input (system prompt, tool definitions, a long document) is byte-for-byte identical to the last call.
bullets: Cost and time-to-first-token both scale with prompt length, every single call
Agents and long chats resend the same large prefix dozens or hundreds of times per session

slides.title: Why re-running the same prefix is pure waste
slides.body: An LLM turns input text into a KV cache — attention keys/values for every token — before it can generate anything. That computation depends only on the tokens before it, not on what comes after.
bullets: If your first 10,000 tokens (system prompt + tool defs + repo context) are unchanged between calls, the model still recomputes their KV cache every time without caching
For a 50-turn agent session with a 10k-token static prefix, that's 500,000 tokens of redundant prefix processing across the session
This redundant work shows up as both direct token cost and added latency before the first output token

slides.title: Cache breakpoints: marking where the prefix stops changing
slides.body: Prompt caching lets you mark one or more 'breakpoints' in your prompt. The provider stores the KV cache up to each breakpoint, keyed on an exact match of every token before it.
bullets: A cache write (first time a prefix is seen) typically costs more than a normal input token — about +25% on Claude's API
A cache hit (reusing a stored prefix) costs far less — about 10% of the normal input token price, i.e. roughly a 90% discount on that portion
Cached entries expire quickly by default (around 5 minutes of inactivity), with an extended option (around 1 hour) available at a added cost
Up to a handful of breakpoints are allowed per request, so you can cache multiple nested prefixes (e.g., system prompt, then tools, then conversation history) independently

slides.title: Worked example: a 50-turn coding agent session
slides.body: Say a coding agent's static prefix (system prompt + tool schemas) is 10,000 tokens, unchanged across 50 turns in one session.
bullets: Without caching: 50 calls x 10,000 tokens = 500,000 prefix tokens billed at full price
With caching: 1 cache write (10,000 x 1.25 = 12,500) + 49 cache reads (49 x 10,000 x 0.1 = 49,000) = 61,500 token-equivalents
That's roughly an 8x reduction in billed tokens for the prefix alone — before counting the saved latency on every one of those 49 calls
The savings only materialize if the cached prefix is reused before it expires — a session that goes idle past the TTL pays the full write cost again

slides.title: Caching isn't identical everywhere
slides.body: The mechanism (reuse a prefix's computed state) is common across major providers, but the controls differ — treat exact numbers for non-Claude providers as approximate.

rows: Explicit cache breakpoints, you choose TTL (5 min default / 1 hr extended)
Automatic caching of repeated prefixes above a length threshold
Discounted cached-input tokens, no manual breakpoints
Explicit cached-content resource you create and reference
Reduced token cost while the cached resource is alive

slides.title: Where caching breaks, quietly
slides.body: Prompt caching rewards very specific prompt discipline, and violating it silently gives you zero savings — with no error message.
bullets: Changing even one token before a breakpoint invalidates the cache for everything after it, forcing a full (costlier) rewrite
Putting user-specific or timestamped content (today's date, a user ID) early in the prompt defeats caching for every later static section
Very short prefixes often fall below the minimum cacheable length and simply can't be cached at all
Caching only discounts prefix *processing* — it does nothing for output generation cost, so verbose responses stay just as expensive
Bursty, low-frequency traffic can let the cache expire between calls, turning every 'cached' call back into a full-price write

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: Order your prompt static-content-first: system instructions and tool definitions before any per-request or user-specific text
Put a cache breakpoint right after the largest stable block you have — that's where the savings compound over a session
Expect roughly a 25% premium on the first write and a ~90% discount on each subsequent hit (Claude's numbers; treat other providers as directionally similar)
Caching helps most for agents, long multi-turn chats, and repeated large-document Q&A — it does nothing for one-off, fully unique prompts

questions.prompt: What actually gets cached in prompt caching?
options: A compressed copy of the raw text
The model's computed attention state (KV cache) for a given prompt prefix
The final generated response, for reuse on identical future prompts
A hash table of synonyms used to shorten the prompt
questions.explanation: Prompt caching stores the KV cache — the attention keys/values the model computed for a prefix — so a later identical prefix can skip that computation instead of being reprocessed.

questions.prompt: What happens if you change one token before your cache breakpoint?
options: Nothing — the cache still applies to the rest
Only that one token is recomputed
The cache misses entirely for everything after that point, and it's recomputed and rewritten at full (plus write-premium) cost
The request is rejected with an error
questions.explanation: Caching requires an exact match of every token before the breakpoint. Any change earlier in the prefix invalidates the cache for all of it — silently, with no error, just no discount.

questions.prompt: Where should you put dynamic, per-request content (like today's date or a user ID) in a cached prompt?
options: As early as possible, before the system prompt
Anywhere — position doesn't matter for caching
As late as possible, after the static system/tool content, so the static prefix stays cacheable
Caching should be disabled whenever any dynamic content exists
questions.explanation: Putting dynamic content early breaks the exact-match requirement for everything after it. Keeping static content first and dynamic content last preserves the cache for the large stable prefix.

posts.title: FlashProve: Proving Which Model Actually Answered You
posts.subtitle: A zkSNARK that checks a 400B MoE model's output without re-running it.
posts.summary: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team built FlashProve, an open research prototype that lets anyone verify a given prompt-and-reply really came from a specific committed set of model weights, without re-running the model. Tested on Llama 4 Maverick (400B, MoE), it proves inference at 110 tokens/sec on one H100 and checks a proof in about 17 seconds — 70-95x slower than normal serving, but 4-40x faster than the next-best prior zkLLM systems.

slides.title: FlashProve: Proving Which Model Actually Answered You
slides.body: Published November 2, 2026 by Anthropic's Frontier Red Team with academic collaborators from EPFL, MIT, and StarkWare, FlashProve is an open-source prototype for 'provable inference' — cryptographic proof that a specific committed model produced a specific reply.
bullets: Targets large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, tested on 400B-parameter Llama 4 Maverick
Prover runs at 110 tokens/sec on a single H100 GPU
Code, Lean formal proofs, and docs released under Apache 2.0

slides.title: You can't prove which model wrote your answer
slides.body: A provider, a routing layer, or an attacker could quietly swap in a cheaper or different model, or tamper with the token stream. Reading the output tells you nothing — a swapped model can produce fluent, plausible text.
bullets: No way today to check 'this exact committed model generated this exact reply'
Matters for model-tier billing, regulation/compliance, tamper detection, and provenance
Output quality alone can't distinguish the real model from a cheaper substitute

slides.title: Commit once offline, prove cheaply online
slides.body: FlashProve splits the work into two phases and exploits MoE sparsity so the prover's cost scales with active parameters, not total parameters.
bullets: Offline: publish a short cryptographic commitment to the weights — pins them down without revealing them
Online: for each request, produce a zkSNARK proof that the committed model maps this prompt to this exact output
Only Maverick's ~17B active params/token are proven, not all 400B — proven one layer-segment at a time to fit one GPU
Built from an interactive oracle proof compiled with hash functions only — no elliptic curves, so it stays post-quantum secure

slides.title: A real run: proving 24 requests end to end
slides.body: On Llama 4 Maverick (400B MoE, 4-bit weights), one commitment covers up to ~16 million requests before it needs to be refreshed.
bullets: Offline commitment: ~39 minutes, done once per model
Online proving: ~223 seconds to prove a batch of 24 requests (1,024 tokens each)
Each proof is ~19 MB; verifying one takes ~17 seconds on 24 CPU threads, ~21 seconds on one thread
Client only needs ~6.5 MB (the commitment) plus the per-request proof — never the weights

slides.title: Fastest zkVM for LLMs yet, but still far from free
slides.body: FlashProve beats every open prior attempt at proving real frontier-scale models by a wide margin, though a commercial, closed system reports it is still faster.

slides.title: What the proof does — and doesn't — guarantee
slides.body: FlashProve is an honest research prototype, not a finished trust system, and the authors are explicit about where it falls short.
bullets: ~70-95x slower per-GPU than normal vLLM serving for the same batch — proving is expensive
Only covers an exact integer version of the weights under greedy decoding; floating-point or sampled outputs, and adversarial prompts, aren't covered
Proofs cap out at 1,024 tokens — far short of real chat or frontier context windows
Zero-knowledge (hiding the weights) depends on trusting the prover's implementation — providers must audit it themselves
Proves hardware served this output, not that the same hardware wasn't also training at the time

slides.title: Verifiable inference is now a tractable research direction
slides.body: FlashProve doesn't make every API call provable today, but it moves frontier-scale provable inference from '14 hours for 1,000 tokens' to 'minutes for a batch' — a 4-40x jump over the best prior open systems.
bullets: MoE sparsity is the key lever: prove the ~17B active params, not the 400B total
Post-quantum by construction — proofs rest on hash functions, not elliptic curves
Correctness properties (completeness, soundness, zero-knowledge) are formally verified in Lean
Next steps the authors flag: longer context, cheaper proving, hiding model architecture too

questions.prompt: Why does FlashProve's prover cost scale with Llama 4 Maverick's ~17B active parameters instead of its full 400B?
options: It only proves the attention layers, not the feed-forward layers
It exploits Mixture-of-Experts sparsity — only the experts actually activated per token need to be proven
It compresses the model to 17B parameters before proving
It samples a random 17B-parameter subset of the weights each time
questions.explanation: Maverick is a 400B-parameter MoE model, but each token only routes through ~17B active parameters. FlashProve proves exactly the computation that ran, so its cost tracks the active path, not the full model — a core reason it's tractable at all.

questions.prompt: What does FlashProve's zero-knowledge property actually hide?
options: The prompt the user sent
The identity of the user making the request
The model's weights — the commitment pins them down without revealing their values
The GPU hardware used to run inference
questions.explanation: The offline commitment lets anyone verify a proof is tied to one fixed set of weights, without those weights ever being disclosed. The zero-knowledge property is specifically about not leaking the weights themselves.

questions.prompt: Roughly how much slower is FlashProve's proving step than just serving the same batch with vLLM?
options: About 2x slower
About 10x slower
About 70-95x slower
About 1,000x slower
questions.explanation: The paper reports roughly 70-95x the per-GPU time of ordinary vLLM serving for the same 24-request batch. That's the real cost of verifiability today — proving isn't free, even though it's far cheaper than prior zkLLM systems.

posts.title: Rotary Position Embeddings: Order Without Addition
posts.subtitle: How RoPE bakes word order into attention by rotating vectors, not adding to them.
posts.summary: Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) give transformers a sense of word order by rotating each query and key vector by an angle proportional to its position, instead of adding a position vector to the embedding. The payoff: the attention score between two tokens ends up depending only on the distance between them, not their absolute positions — and it's used in LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, and most modern open LLMs.

slides.title: Rotary Position Embeddings: Order Without Addition
slides.body: Self-attention on its own can't tell 'dog bites man' from 'man bites dog' — it's permutation-invariant. RoPE fixes that by rotating each query/key vector by an angle that depends on its position, instead of adding a separate position signal.
bullets: Used by LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, GPT-NeoX, and most modern open-weight LLMs
Encodes position by rotation, not addition
Makes attention scores depend on relative distance, not absolute position

slides.title: Attention has no built-in notion of order
slides.body: Dot-product attention computes a score for every pair of tokens regardless of where they sit in the sequence. Without extra position information, shuffling the input tokens wouldn't change attention's output at all.
bullets: Original fix: add a learned or sinusoidal position vector to each token's embedding
Absolute position embeddings generalize poorly past the lengths seen in training
They also mix position into the embedding permanently, instead of letting attention reason about *relative* distance directly

slides.title: Rotate query and key vectors by angle m·θ
slides.body: RoPE pairs up adjacent dimensions of each query/key vector and rotates each pair by an angle proportional to the token's position m, using a different fixed frequency θ per pair (lower dimensions rotate fast, higher dimensions rotate slowly — a Fourier-like spread).
bullets: Query at position m and key at position n are each rotated by mθ and nθ before the dot product
Rotation matrices satisfy R(m)·R(n)ᵗ = R(m-n) — rotating both vectors is equivalent to rotating by their difference
So Q(m)·K(n) ends up as a function of (m - n) only, never m or n individually
No extra vector is added anywhere; position lives entirely in the rotation applied at attention time

slides.title: Worked example: two tokens, one 2D pair
slides.body: Take one rotated dimension-pair with base angle θ. A query at position 5 and a key at position 2 each get rotated before their dot product is taken.
bullets: Query vector rotated by 5θ; key vector rotated by 2θ
Their dot product reduces to |q||k|·cos(5θ - 2θ) = |q||k|·cos(3θ)
Swap to query at position 9, key at position 6 — same distance (3), same cos(3θ), same attention contribution
The model never needs to see '5' or '2' directly — only the gap between them shows up in the score

slides.title: RoPE vs. the alternatives

rows: Subtracts a distance penalty from attention scores
Yes, via a fixed linear bias

slides.title: RoPE isn't free of limits
slides.body: Rotation gives a clean relative-position property, but it doesn't automatically solve long-context generalization.
bullets: Accuracy degrades sharply once sequence length exceeds what the model was trained on — the rotation angles go to parts of the circle the model never learned to use
Fixing this needs explicit extensions: position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, or YaRN, which rescale the rotation frequencies for longer contexts
The base frequency θ (often 10,000) is a tuned hyperparameter — the wrong value hurts either short-range precision or long-range reach
Pure rotation carries no information about absolute position at all, which some tasks (e.g. knowing you're at the very start of a document) still need

slides.title: Why RoPE won out
slides.body: RoPE became the default positional scheme in modern open LLMs because it gets relative-position awareness essentially for free, with no extra parameters and no separate position vector to learn.
bullets: Encodes position by rotating Q/K, not by adding a position vector
Attention score depends only on relative distance (m - n), by construction
Needs explicit scaling tricks (YaRN, NTK-aware, position interpolation) to extrapolate past training length
Default choice in LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, and most current open-weight LLM families

questions.prompt: What does RoPE do differently from classic absolute position embeddings?
options: It adds a larger position vector to the token embedding
It rotates the query and key vectors by a position-dependent angle instead of adding anything
It removes positional information entirely and relies on causal masking alone
It only encodes position for the first token in the sequence
questions.explanation: RoPE applies a rotation to Q and K at attention time, rather than adding a learned or sinusoidal vector to the embedding. The rotation is what makes the resulting attention score depend only on relative position.

questions.prompt: Why does Q(m)·K(n) end up depending only on (m - n) under RoPE?
options: Because the rotation matrices are randomly initialized and average out
Because rotating both vectors by their own position is mathematically equivalent to rotating one vector by the difference in positions
Because RoPE clips the maximum sequence length to a fixed constant
Because the dot product ignores position entirely once vectors are normalized
questions.explanation: Rotation matrices compose: R(m)·R(n)ᵗ = R(m-n). So rotating the query by mθ and the key by nθ before taking their dot product leaves a result that's a function of only the gap (m-n), never the absolute positions themselves.

questions.prompt: A model trained with RoPE on 4K-token sequences is run on a 32K-token prompt and accuracy drops sharply past 4K tokens. What's the standard fix?
options: Retrain the attention mechanism to use absolute embeddings instead
Apply a scaling technique such as position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, or YaRN to adapt the rotation frequencies
Remove RoPE and use no positional encoding at all
Increase the model's hidden dimension size
questions.explanation: RoPE's rotation angles only cover the range seen during training. Techniques like position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, and YaRN rescale those frequencies so the model can handle longer sequences without retraining from scratch.

posts.title: PDD Kit: Proofs, Not Just Tests, for AI-Written Code
posts.subtitle: Microsoft's prototype makes a coding agent prove its code, not just pass tests for it.
posts.summary: Microsoft Research's PDD Kit pairs a coding agent with the Verus verifier so that Rust code an agent writes comes with a machine-checked proof, not just passing tests. A 'vibe verification' mutation check catches specs that verify but constrain nothing, and a six-function trusted boundary marks exactly where proof hands off to tests.

slides.title: When agents write code faster than anyone can review it
slides.body: Coding agents can now produce tens of thousands of lines per feature. Microsoft Research's PDD Kit is a research prototype that has an agent prove its Rust code correct against a formal spec, instead of asking a human to read all of it.
bullets: Proof-Driven Development: an agent writes a spec, the code, and a proof — not just a plan
Uses Verus, a Rust verifier built on the Z3 SMT solver
Demoed on a ~5,000-line Rust 'Pet Store' app (Axum + SQLite + Leptos/WASM)

slides.title: Tests sample inputs; review doesn't scale
slides.body: Unit and end-to-end tests check a finite set of cases. A coding agent that writes a login handler can pass every test in the suite and still be wrong on an input nobody thought to try — and nobody is reading all of it line by line anymore.
bullets: Agents now generate code faster than humans can meaningfully review it
Passing tests are evidence of correctness, not proof of it
The riskiest code (auth, payments, permissions) is exactly where a missed edge case costs the most

slides.title: Three steps: plan, prove, ship
slides.body: PDD Kit splits the work the way Spec Kit splits spec-driven development, but for formal methods instead of plain-language specs.
bullets: pdd-plan: asks clarifying questions, then writes an 'intent artifact' linking plain-language intent to formal specs and tests
pdd-prove: a coding agent writes the implementation and a Verus proof; an LLM reviewer also checks for gaps
pdd-ship: wires the Verus check into CI alongside the existing empirical tests
Anything that can't be formalized (a database, bcrypt, a clock) becomes an explicitly trusted, contract-wrapped function instead

slides.title: 'Vibe verification': a spec that proves nothing
slides.body: A proof is only as good as the spec it proves. PDD Kit's authors coined 'vibe verification' for specs that technically verify but rule out almost nothing — a common failure mode when a model writes its own spec.
bullets: Mutation check: pdd-prove plants one deliberate bug per 'ensures' clause (e.g. reject every login) in a scratch copy
Verus must reject each mutant on the exact clause it's supposed to constrain
A mutant that still passes means that clause is vacuous — reported back as a gap to fix
Ghost code (spec-only, erased at compile time) and uninterpreted functions model what the proof can't see, like 'does this password match the hash'

slides.title: Worked example: proving a login handler
slides.body: The Pet Store demo scoped the proof to backend/src/handlers/auth.rs, with two developer requirements: tokens issue only for a correct password, and admin tokens only for admin accounts.
bullets: Proved end-to-end: login_flow, login_core, lookup_target, decide_login, issue_token — 8 'ensures' clauses total
Explicitly trusted (6 pieces, each needing developer sign-off): the two DB lookups, check_password (wraps bcrypt::verify), generate_token, expiry_from_now (24h = 86,400s), and the handler shell
Running the proof hardened the code and surfaced existing bugs the test suite had missed
The developer chose the stricter option (proving the async login_flow itself) over the easier option of just trusting the handler

slides.title: Testing vs. proof-driven development
slides.body: PDD Kit doesn't replace tests — untestable-by-proof pieces (DB, crypto, clocks, UI) still rely on them. It adds a second, stronger guarantee on top for the logic that matters most.

rows: Holds for the cases you wrote
Holds for every input allowed by the spec
A case you forgot to test
The spec itself not matching real intent
Rust code provable in Verus; everything else falls back to tests
Seconds for a small module, minutes for a larger one

slides.title: Where it breaks down — and when not to reach for it
slides.body: PDD Kit is explicitly a research prototype, and its authors are careful to flag exactly how far the guarantee actually extends.
bullets: Rust-only today: the whole pipeline depends on Verus, so other languages need porting or bindings first
A proof shows code matches its spec — not that the spec matches what the developer actually meant
The guarantee is only as strong as the 6 trusted, unproven pieces; check_password and the DB lookups carry most of the real risk
Not proved in the demo: whether the login future ever completes, panic behavior on bad clock values, or timing/rate of attempts
The authors explicitly warn that 'fully verified' is easy to oversell — this proves one handler, not the whole app

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: PDD Kit is an early, narrow but real demonstration that agent-written code can carry machine-checked guarantees — if a team is willing to pay the proof tax on the parts that matter most.
bullets: Proof-Driven Development binds an agent to a formal spec, not just a plan — a stronger leash than review-by-reading
The trusted boundary (6 functions in the demo) is where all remaining risk concentrates — review that, not the proved code
'Vibe verification' is the same lesson as vibe coding: a check that always passes isn't actually checking anything
Worth it today only for the highest-stakes Rust logic (auth, payments, permissions) — not a general replacement for tests

questions.prompt: What does a Verus proof in PDD Kit actually guarantee?
options: That the code has no bugs anywhere in the application
That the code satisfies its formal spec for every input the spec allows, not just the inputs a test suite happens to cover
That the code passed all existing unit tests
That the spec correctly captures what the developer intended
questions.explanation: A Verus proof holds for every input permitted by the spec, which is stronger than tests (which only check specific cases). But it does NOT guarantee the spec matches real intent, nor does it cover the trusted, unproven pieces like bcrypt or the database.

questions.prompt: What is 'vibe verification', and how does PDD Kit catch it?
options: Code that compiles but was never run
A spec that technically verifies but constrains almost nothing — caught by planting a bug per 'ensures' clause and checking Verus rejects it
A proof that takes too long to run in CI
Trusting a function without a contract
questions.explanation: Models tend to write weak specs that pass trivially. PDD Kit's mutation check plants one deliberate bug per ensures clause; if Verus still accepts the mutated code, that clause isn't actually constraining anything and gets flagged as a gap.

questions.prompt: In the Pet Store demo, where does the real risk sit even after the login logic is 'proved'?
options: Nowhere — the proof covers 100% of the application's risk
In the six explicitly trusted functions (like check_password and the DB lookups), which are assumed correct and backed only by tests, not proofs
In the Leptos frontend, which was also fully proved
In the CI pipeline configuration
questions.explanation: login_flow and related functions were proved, but six pieces — including check_password (wrapping bcrypt) and the two database lookups — were explicitly marked trusted with assumed contracts. Those are backed only by tests, so they're where undetected bugs can still hide.

posts.title: MCP Sampling: Letting the Server Borrow the Client's Model
posts.subtitle: Most MCP traffic flows one way. Sampling is the exception — the server calls back into the model.
posts.summary: MCP servers are normally thin integrations with no LLM of their own. Sampling lets a server send a 'sampling/createMessage' request back over the same connection, asking the client's model to generate a completion it can use mid-task — inverting the usual client-calls-server direction, with the client still in control of cost, model choice, and (optionally) human approval.

slides.title: The one MCP request that flows backwards
slides.body: Normally, an MCP client calls a server's tools. Sampling flips that: the server asks the client to run a piece of reasoning for it, using whatever model backs that session.
bullets: A server-initiated request: 'sampling/createMessage'
Lets a tool-only server use an LLM without holding its own API key
The client stays in control of which model runs and whether a human signs off

slides.title: Most MCP servers have no model of their own
slides.body: An MCP server is often a thin wrapper — a Slack connector, a file-search index, a ticketing API. It's great at fetching and acting on data, but if a step in its own logic needs judgment (summarize, classify, decide), it hits a wall.
bullets: Giving every server its own API key duplicates billing and model choice the user already made elsewhere
Hardcoding a specific model inside the server locks it to that vendor and that cost tier
Without sampling, servers either skip the reasoning step or return raw, unprocessed data for the agent to sort out

slides.title: The mechanism: a request inside the response
slides.body: Sampling is a capability both sides negotiate at connection time. Once enabled, the server can pause its own tool call and issue a nested request back to the client.
bullets: Server sends 'sampling/createMessage' with messages, an optional system prompt, maxTokens, and modelPreferences (cost/speed/quality hints, not a hard model name)
Client intercepts the request — it can show the user what's being asked before anything runs
Client picks a model (its own choice, not the server's) and returns the completion over the same connection
Server resumes its original tool logic using that result, then returns its final output to the agent loop

slides.title: Worked example: summarizing search hits before returning them
slides.body: An MCP email-search server finds 40 messages matching a query. Returning all 40 bodies would flood the agent's context window.
bullets: Server issues a sampling request per message (or a batched one): 'write a one-line summary of this email'
Client routes each request to whichever model is backing the current session — the server never sees which model that is
Server collects the summaries and returns 40 compact lines instead of 40 full email bodies
The agent's context budget is spent on the final digest, not on raw data the server already had

slides.title: Sampling vs. Elicitation — easy to confuse
slides.body: Both are server-initiated, both pause the tool call to ask for something — but they ask different parties for different things.

rows: A structured decision or missing input
Confirm a destructive action, fill a missing field

slides.title: Tradeoffs and pitfalls
slides.body: Sampling is powerful precisely because it's indirect — which is also where its sharp edges are.
bullets: Human-in-the-loop approval (recommended by the spec) adds real latency if every call needs sign-off — fine for one summary, costly for forty
Servers must write model-agnostic prompts: modelPreferences are hints, not guarantees, so the server can't assume a specific model's quirks
Sampling tokens bill against the client's/host's budget, not the server's — a chatty server can quietly burn the user's quota
Not every MCP client implements sampling yet; a well-built server must degrade gracefully (skip the step or return raw data) when the capability isn't offered

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: Sampling is what lets 'dumb' MCP servers stay dumb — and borrow intelligence only when they need it, from whoever is already paying for it.
bullets: It's the one MCP flow that runs server-to-client instead of client-to-server
It decouples 'who hosts the model' from 'who needs a completion' — servers never need their own API key
Pair it with Elicitation (asks the human) and Roots (filesystem boundaries) to see MCP's three server-initiated features as a set
Design servers to work (just less well) when a client doesn't support sampling — never assume it's there

questions.prompt: What problem does MCP's sampling feature solve for a server?
options: It lets the server store data persistently between sessions
It lets a server with no LLM of its own request a completion from the client, instead of needing its own API key and model
It speeds up the server's database queries
It lets the server bypass the client's permission system entirely
questions.explanation: Sampling exists because most MCP servers are thin integrations without their own model access. Instead of requiring every server to hold an API key and pick a model, sampling lets the server ask the client to run the completion using whatever model the session already has.

questions.prompt: Who actually chooses which model runs a sampling request?
options: The server, via the modelPreferences field
The client/host, which treats modelPreferences only as hints, not a binding model name
The MCP protocol itself, which hardcodes a default model
Whichever party sends the request first
questions.explanation: modelPreferences lets a server express priorities (cost, speed, quality) as hints, but the client decides which actual model backs the completion. Servers must write prompts that work regardless of which model answers.

questions.prompt: How does Sampling differ from Elicitation?
options: They're two names for the same request method
Sampling asks the client's LLM to generate a completion; Elicitation asks the human user for structured input or a decision
Sampling is client-initiated; Elicitation is server-initiated
Elicitation is only used for billing purposes
questions.explanation: Both are server-initiated requests, but they target different parties: sampling (sampling/createMessage) asks the client's model to generate text, while elicitation (elicitation/create) asks the human directly — e.g. to confirm a destructive action or supply a missing parameter.

posts.title: Why Most AI Safety Evals Measure the Wrong Thing
posts.subtitle: Anthropic's playbook borrows psychology's replication-crisis fixes to make safety scores trustworthy.
posts.summary: A safety claim is only as sound as the eval behind it, and most AI safety evals quietly measure the wrong thing. Anthropic's new framework borrows construct validity, preregistration, and grader validation from psychology's replication crisis to make safety scores reproducible instead of decorative.

slides.title: The Eval Said It Was Safe. Was It?
slides.body: Anthropic's new playbook borrows hard lessons from psychology's replication crisis to fix how AI safety is actually measured.

slides.title: Safety Evals Are Easier to Fake Than to Build
slides.body: A model's 'safety score' is only as solid as the eval behind it, and most evals are shakier than they look.
bullets: Evals can be gamed, poorly documented, or sensitive to formatting: multiple-choice vs. open-ended, even answer order, can swing results
Single-turn harmless-response rates on the API already sit at 94-98% for recent models, so the easy wins are gone and the signal is thinner
The fix borrows directly from psychology's replication crisis: preregistration, better measurement, shared tooling

slides.title: Construct Validity: Are You Measuring the Right Thing?
slides.body: A safety eval should measure whether a model avoids causing harm, not whether it refuses. Picking the wrong proxy wrecks the eval before data collection even starts.
bullets: For self-harm conversations, refusal is often the WRONG construct; the safer behavior is staying engaged and directing users to support
A system-prompt fix lifted claude.ai's appropriate-response rate on self-harm transcripts from 60% (raw API) to 94%
Dual-use domains like phishing need paired harmful/benign prompts: good answers help defenders while withholding operational detail

slides.title: Four Stages: Safety First, Design, Run, Report
bullets: Safety first: staff domain experts (psychologists, biologists) alongside methods experts; risky cyber evals run sandboxed, offline, monitored live
Design: match the design to the question; observational evals describe behavior, causal evals isolate whether an intervention actually works
Run: guard against data contamination and reward hacking; graders use atomic yes/no criteria validated against human labels
Report: break results down by category, publish confidence intervals, and document full configs so runs can be reproduced

slides.title: The Romance-Scam Eval: Why One Bad Turn Fails the Whole Conversation
slides.body: No single message is an obvious violation; the harm only surfaces across the arc of a multi-turn conversation.
bullets: Transcripts simulate a scammer probing for vulnerable targets over many turns; the whole conversation fails if ANY single turn is inappropriate
That's harder to game than a one-shot prompt, but needs bigger samples: a 100-item floor for complex multi-turn evals, 1,000 for simple single-turn ones
Coverage check: single-turn suites alone span 16 policy areas and 7 languages across multiple product surfaces

slides.title: The Same Model, Measured Two Different Ways
slides.body: Same model, same questions; the deployment surface alone swung the score by 34 points.

rows: Self-harm transcripts, raw API (no system prompt)
Single-turn harmless responses, API, recent models

slides.title: When the Eval Itself Is Broken
slides.body: Bad evals don't only make models look safer than they are; sometimes they make models look worse, or make real gaps invisible.
bullets: An audit of a leading coding benchmark found many tasks underspecified, with graders rejecting genuinely correct solutions
Opus 5 scored 98% and Opus 5.5 scored 94% on one romance-scam eval, a gap that looks real but wasn't statistically significant
Don't trust a score until the grader is checked: it should agree with human experts about as often as experts agree with each other
Treat eval sets as living documents; rerun continuously during training, not just as a pre-release checkbox

slides.title: Build Evals Like You'd Build a Science
bullets: Define the construct before collecting data; 'refusal' is often the wrong proxy for 'safe'
Validate graders against humans, report confidence intervals, and preregister the analysis plan
A 34-point swing between API and product surface means deployment context is part of the safety story, not an afterthought
Borrowed tools like Inspect, preregistration, and paired comparisons are turning AI safety evaluation into a replicable science

questions.prompt: In Anthropic's framework, why is 'refusal rate' often the wrong metric for a self-harm safety eval?
options: Because refusing is always unsafe
Because the right behavior is often to stay engaged and redirect to support, not refuse
Because refusal rates can't be measured reliably
Because only jailbreak evals use refusal rate
questions.explanation: Refusal measures compliance, not harm. For self-harm conversations, the safer behavior is often continued, careful engagement that steers the user toward support, so refusal is the wrong construct to optimize for.

questions.prompt: Opus 5 scored 98% and Opus 5.5 scored 94% on a romance-scam eval. Why does the post caution against treating that as a real regression?
options: Because the eval was only run once
Because multi-turn eval confidence intervals can exceed +/-10 points, so a 4-point gap isn't necessarily significant
Because Opus 5.5 is a newer model and newer models always score lower
Because romance-scam evals don't apply to newer models
questions.explanation: Multi-turn evals carry wide confidence intervals, here over +/-10 points, so a small gap between two scores can be noise rather than a genuine capability or safety difference.

questions.prompt: What does it mean to 'validate a grader' before trusting an eval's score?
options: Running the eval on more GPUs
Checking that the grader's judgments agree with human expert labels about as often as experts agree with each other
Making sure the grader is a larger model than the one being tested
Translating the eval into multiple languages
questions.explanation: An automated grader is only trustworthy once it's benchmarked against human judgment using chance-corrected agreement; otherwise the eval might just be measuring the grader's own biases.

posts.title: StudentSim: AI Tutors Trained Against a Simulated Student
posts.subtitle: Microsoft Research built a per-student simulator and used it as a reward signal to train sharper AI tutors.
posts.summary: Microsoft Research's StudentSim trains a personalized simulator for each student in two stages — shared patterns first, then individual specialization — and scores it on whether it matches a real student's answers and reacts correctly to tutoring feedback. Used as an RL reward signal, it trained a chess tutor to 90.5% accuracy, beating both a supervised-only baseline and a GPT-5.4-reward baseline, though the authors are clear it's a research system, not a classroom product yet.

slides.title: Grading a Tutor Needs a Student
slides.body: You can't know if AI tutoring advice actually helps without watching what happens after a student reads it — and that's the part researchers couldn't cheaply measure.

slides.title: Role-Play Students Are Too Smart
slides.body: Two broken shortcuts dominated AI-tutor evaluation before StudentSim.
bullets: Human studies measure real learning but are slow and expensive to run per tutoring strategy.
Asking an LLM to 'pretend to be a struggling student' sounds right but reasons far above that student's real level — making weak tutors look good.
Classic knowledge-tracing models track ability over time but can't take natural-language tutor feedback as input at all.

slides.title: Two-Stage Training: Pooled, Then Personal
slides.body: StudentSim builds one simulator per student instead of one generic 'student' persona.
bullets: Stage 1: train on de-identified records pooled across many students to learn shared patterns — common errors, typical revisions after feedback.
Stage 2: specialize the model on one individual student's own history, which fixes the sparse-data problem per-student records alone would cause.
Scored on two axes: behavioral fidelity (does it match the real student's held-out answers?) and guidance responsiveness (does it update correctly after reading tutor feedback?).

slides.title: Three Domains, Same Two Tests
slides.body: The approach was validated outside a single narrow task.
bullets: Chess: predicting a player's next move and how it changes after coaching.
Second-language English writing: generating essays with a learner's own error patterns and predicting their corrections.
Math: predicting multiple-choice answers and how they shift after an explanation.

slides.title: The Numbers, in Chess
slides.body: StudentSim beat both a frontier general-purpose LLM and a dedicated chess model at modeling a specific player.

slides.title: Using It as an RL Reward Signal
slides.body: The real payoff: StudentSim can train the tutor, not just grade it after the fact.
bullets: A chess tutor trained with StudentSim as its simulated-student reward hit 90.5% accuracy.
A supervised tutor with no RL at all reached only 75.7%.
A tutor rewarded by GPT-5.4's role-play judgments reached just 71.6%.
Blind expert evaluators — not told which tutor was which — also rated the StudentSim-trained tutor higher on guidance quality and personalization.

slides.title: Not a Classroom Product Yet
slides.body: The authors are explicit about the limits.
bullets: StudentSim is a research system — it has not been deployed in real classrooms.
It doesn't replace human studies, which are still required for learning outcomes, safety, and usability.
It needs rich per-student trace data; domains without that history can't be modeled the same way.
Open questions: longer learning trajectories, more subjects, and whether simulator gains actually translate to real student outcomes.

slides.title: Why This Matters
slides.body: Cheap, personalized simulators turn tutor evaluation from a slow human study into a fast, repeatable test loop — and turn 'does this feedback help?' into a reward signal you can actually train against.
bullets: Pool-then-personalize beats either pure pooling or pure per-student training alone.
Matching a real student beats role-play — a frontier LLM pretending to be a student still reasons like itself.
A good simulator can train the tutor via RL, not just evaluate it after the fact.
Still a research prototype: treat the gains as promising, not proven in real classrooms.

questions.prompt: What does StudentSim's 'guidance responsiveness' score actually measure?
options: How fast the simulator runs on GPU hardware
Whether the simulator updates its answer appropriately after reading tutor feedback
How many students were in the training set
Whether the simulator can generate essays in multiple languages
questions.explanation: Behavioral fidelity checks if the simulator matches a student's real held-out answers; guidance responsiveness checks if it reacts correctly once it's shown tutoring feedback — the two failure modes a simulator needs to avoid.

questions.prompt: In the chess RL experiment, which reward signal produced the most accurate tutor?
options: A supervised tutor trained with no reinforcement learning at all (75.7%)
A tutor rewarded by GPT-5.4 role-playing a student (71.6%)
A tutor rewarded by StudentSim's personalized simulator (90.5%)
Direct feedback from human chess coaches in real time
questions.explanation: StudentSim-as-reward beat both the no-RL baseline and the GPT-5.4-as-judge baseline by a wide margin, showing a personalized simulator gives a better training signal than a generic LLM pretending to be a student.

questions.prompt: Why can't older knowledge-tracing models fill the same role as StudentSim?
options: They are too computationally expensive to run
They track student ability over time but generally can't take natural-language tutor guidance as input
They only work for chess, never for math or writing
They require a live internet connection to function
questions.explanation: Classic knowledge tracing is good at modeling ability trends from right/wrong answers, but it isn't built to read arbitrary natural-language feedback and predict how that specific input changes a student's next answer — the exact gap StudentSim targets.
